item.title: Differentiation Rule: Derivatives of Logarithmic Functions
item.description:
A logarithm is the inverse of an exponential, so its derivative comes from one implicit differentiation of . Everything else in this note follows from three facts. First, the derivative carries a constant factor that disappears exactly when . Second, the chain rule turns into the relative rate , and this survives absolute values. Third, the logarithm converts products, quotients and powers into sums, which is what makes logarithmic differentiation work. The same derivative at also produces the classical limit formulas for .

1 The Derivative of

1.1 Derivation by implicit differentiation

Let , , and for . By definition, Assume is a differentiable function of (this is justified by the inverse function theorem, since is differentiable with nonzero derivative ). Differentiate both sides with respect to , using and the chain rule:

ImportantResult 1

Write the denominator as , never as “”, which reads as .

1.2 Derivation by change of base

Since and is a constant, This route is shorter, but it depends on already knowing . The implicit route depends only on the exponential derivative. Keep track of which fact is proved from which; the dependency order matters again in the section on .

1.3 A structural observation: every logarithm is a rescaled

Change of base says . So all logarithm functions have the same shape and differ only by a vertical scale factor. Their derivatives differ by the same factor. In particular the slope at is , and it equals precisely when .

2 The Natural Logarithm

2.1 Result

Putting in Result 1 and using :

ImportantResult 2

2.2 Why calculus prefers base

The precise statement is not “with we can ignore the base”. The base is still . The point is that the derivative formula carries no extra constant factor , because . The exponential side says the same thing: reduces to .

Three equivalent ways to characterize by this normalization:

Viewpoint Characterization of
Exponential the unique base with , i.e. slope of at equals
Logarithm the unique base with slope of at equal to
Scaling the base for which needs no rescaling to have derivative

The first two are mirror images: the graphs of and are reflections across , which swaps the point with and turns a slope into . Slope is the fixed point of that reciprocal.

2.3 Writing derivatives as equalities between functions

A common notational slip is writing “”. The first equality is between functions, the second confuses a function with its derivative. The correct chain is

3 Combining with the Chain Rule

3.1 The logarithmic derivative

If is differentiable and , the chain rule gives

ImportantResult 3

The quantity is the relative rate of change of : the rate of change per unit of current size. Taking a logarithm converts absolute change into relative change. This is the calculus behind percentage changes, growth rates, and decibels.

3.2 Two standard shapes

  • Logarithm outside: .
  • Logarithm inside: for , the outer function is the square root, giving .

For a nested logarithm such as , each layer contributes one factor: and the domain is found from the innermost condition outward: .

4 The Absolute Value:

4.1 Derivation

is defined for every . Split by sign: For the derivative is . For the chain rule gives

ImportantResult 4

4.2 Why no case split is needed afterward

The general form follows from Result 4 and the chain rule. The sign of cancels between numerator and denominator, so a single formula covers both signs. For example, wherever . Splitting into and is only necessary when differentiating itself, not its logarithm.

Geometrically, is even, so its derivative must be odd; is odd. The two branches are mirror images and have opposite slopes at .

5 Simplify Before Differentiating

5.1 Laws of logarithms as a differentiation tool

Using before differentiating replaces product and quotient rules with sums. Compare two routes for

  • Quotient route. Chain rule on the whole quotient requires a quotient derivative and a careful cancellation. It is easy to cancel one factor of too many.
  • Split route.

Similar one-line simplifications:

Function Rewrite Derivative
(no split)

The last entry is , the inverse hyperbolic cosine.

5.2 The domain caveat when splitting

Log laws hold as identities only where every logarithm on both sides is defined. Splitting can silently shrink the domain. Consider Since whenever , the domain is . Writing requires and loses the interval . The correct split uses an absolute value: Result 4 makes the derivative formula identical, which is why the slip is invisible in the final answer but matters for the stated domain.

6 Logarithmic Differentiation

6.1 The procedure

For built from products, quotients and powers:

  1. Take of both sides.
  2. Expand with the laws of logarithms.
  3. Differentiate implicitly with respect to ; the left side becomes .
  4. Multiply by and substitute the original expression.

6.2 Why it works

The logarithm is a homomorphism from multiplication to addition. For The relative rate of a product is the weighted sum of the relative rates of its factors. The product rule and quotient rule are special cases of this identity.

6.3 Why rather than

may be negative on parts of its domain, for example for , or anything containing or . There is undefined, while is fine. Result 4 guarantees the computation is unchanged, which is why many worked solutions omit the bars. Where the method does not apply at all; those points must be checked directly from the original function.

6.4 Variable base and variable exponent

For with , neither the power rule nor the exponential rule applies. Logarithmic differentiation gives Equivalently . The domain requires , since a real power with a non-integer exponent of a negative number is undefined.

The structure is revealing. The two terms are exactly what one would get by treating the exponent as constant (power rule: ) and by treating the base as constant (exponential rule: ), then adding them. For :

Treat as Rule Contribution
exponent frozen power rule
base frozen exponential rule
both vary sum

This “differentiate each slot separately and add” pattern is a first appearance of the multivariable chain rule.

8 Higher Derivatives

8.1 A closed form for

Let . Then , , , and in general Proof by induction. The case holds. If it holds for , differentiating multiplies by : The single factor updates the sign and the factorial at the same time.

8.2

Claim. For every integer , , where .

Proof by induction. For , . Assume the claim for . Since and is a polynomial of degree , it is annihilated by . Therefore For this gives . The mechanism: each differentiation lowers the power of in front of , the polynomial debris dies after enough derivatives, and the last derivative falls on itself.

9 as a Limit

9.1 Logical order

The direction of proof is: Using any later statement to prove an earlier one is circular.

9.2 Step 1: the derivative of at

Let . By the definition of the derivative and Result 2, The proof ends here. Evaluating by the formula is the whole argument.

WarningCircular reasoning trap

Rewriting and then invoking to conclude assumes the very limit that this step is used to establish.

9.3 Step 2: the limit for

From Step 1, . Since is continuous, Restricting to with :

9.4 Step 3: as a limit

For fixed and large (so that ), because and Step 1 applies. By continuity of , This argument works for every real , negative included, and needs neither a substitution (which would not be an integer) nor the continuity of .

9.5 How fast is the convergence?

Expanding with , The error decays only like : one more correct digit costs ten times as many compounding steps.

10 Connection: Logarithmic Derivatives in Link Budgets

Decibels are logarithms, so their derivatives are relative rates. With Result 1 and , A change in linear power is about dB, regardless of the power level.

For Shannon capacity , which decays like : diminishing returns in linear SNR. Measured per decibel instead, with and , At high SNR, every dB adds about bits per second: the familiar “one bit per hertz per 3 dB” rule, read directly off a logarithmic derivative.

11 Self-Check Toolkit

  • Sign and monotonicity. is increasing, so has the sign of where .

  • Special value. Evaluate at a convenient point, often where , and compare with a difference quotient.
  • Homogeneity. In above, is dimensionless, so must scale like ; does, while does not.
  • Two routes. Differentiate once directly and once after splitting with log laws; the results must agree after simplification.
  • Domain transcription. After finding conditions such as , copy them into the final interval notation literally: .

12 Common Pitfalls

item.title: Differentiation Rule: Derivatives of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
item.description:
An inverse trigonometric function is built in two steps: restrict a trigonometric function to an interval on which it is strictly monotone, then invert it. Every derivative in this note comes from one computation. Differentiate implicitly to get , then rewrite in terms of with a Pythagorean identity. The identity determines only up to sign, and the range of the inverse function fixes the sign. That single observation explains every formula, every excluded point, and every convention dispute below.

1 Defining the Inverse Functions

1.1 Why a restriction is needed

A function has an inverse exactly when it is one-to-one. Sine, cosine and tangent are periodic, so each value is attained infinitely often and no inverse exists on the full domain. The remedy is to restrict each function to an interval on which it is strictly monotone and still attains every value of its range. The standard (principal) choices are:

Function Restricted to Inverse Domain of inverse Range of inverse

Each inverse is defined by an equivalence that states the range condition explicitly:

The range condition is not decoration. It is exactly the information that the equation alone does not contain, and every sign decision below comes from it.

The notation means the inverse function, not . Graphically, the inverse is the reflection of the restricted graph across the line (?@fig-inverses).

1.2 Cancellation equations

The two compositions behave differently:

The first holds on the whole domain of . The second holds only on the restricted interval: for any real , is the unique angle in with the same sine as . For example,

Over all of , the map is a triangle wave of period that agrees with only on (?@fig-sawtooth). The same pattern holds for cosine on and tangent on .

1.3 Continuity

A strictly monotone function on an interval whose image is an interval has no jumps, because a jump would leave a gap in the image. Each inverse above is strictly monotone and its image is the restriction interval, so , and are continuous on their domains. Continuity is the hinge of the differentiability proof below.

3.3 Connection to frequency shift

In the Fourier domain . Multiplying a signal by (modulation) shifts the spectrum . In the time domain the same fact reads

Multiplying by an exponential translates the differentiation operator. This is the mechanism behind removing the carrier in baseband-equivalent models, seen from the derivative side.

4 Simplify Before Differentiating

The quotient rule is a last resort. Rewriting first usually shortens the work and reduces error.

After division, constants vanish under differentiation and only a simple remainder term needs work.

Keep denominators factored. The quotient-rule denominator is always ; leave it as rather than . Factored form preserves sign, domain, and cancellation information.

Most errors in differentiation come not from the rules but from the algebra before and after them. Each check below takes seconds.

8 Common Pitfalls

  • Double negatives. When a negative constant multiplies a derivative that itself produces a minus sign, one sign tends to disappear. Factor the constant’s minus out and attach it at the end.

item.title: Linear Programming Approach
item.description:
1 Usage

Each node is in the following order.

  1. Question: Node title.
  2. The first question to think of: A question to answer yourself before starting judo. Judo proceeds in the order of answering this question.
  3. Answer: One or two sentences.
  4. Derivation / Proof: This section is folded. The justification for each line appears to its right. Try writing the derivation yourself first, then unfold it.
  5. Significance: It is folded. What this result enables in the next step.
  6. ↓ Go Down / ↑ Go Up: Child/Parent Node.

For nodes marked with ✍, the guidance question is placed first, and the solution is folded separately.

Common notation: , , represent the number of features, . Vector and matrix inequalities are element-wise. means that all elements are positive.

2 Entire Tree

  • 0. Starting Point: Can the Bellman equation be solved by optimization rather than iteration? → Section 3.1
  • I. Optimization Formula: The unique optimal solution for st is → Section 4.1
    • Three inequalities of the proof → Section 4.1.1
    • Tools used: Monotonicity, iterative limits, positive weighted sum → Section 4.1.2
  • II. Conversion to LP: LP with constraints when max is removed → Section 5.1
    • Two directions of equivalence → Section 5.1.1
    • ’s role → Section 5.1.2
    • Policy Evaluation LP → Section 5.1.3
  • III. Duality: dual LP has variables and constraints → Section 6.1
    • Lagrangian Theorem (reversing the order of summation) → Section 6.1.1
    • ✍ weak duality → Section 6.1.2
    • ✍ is the discount share measure → Section 6.1.3
    • Complementary margin and policy restoration → Section 6.1.4
  • IV. Approximate LP: → Section 7.1
    • Why is the approximate solution above → Section 7.1.1
  • V. Q-function: → Section 8.1
    • Why → Section 8.1.1
    • Bellman equation of Q → Section 8.1.2
    • Monotonality and contraction of → Section 8.1.3

1 Usage

Each node is in the following order.

  1. Question: Node title.
  2. Question to Think of First: A question to answer yourself before looking at the answer.
  3. Answer: One or two sentences or a short expression.

For nodes marked with ✍, the guidance question is placed first, and the solution is folded separately.

The central question of this topic is one: What must be learned to solve the optimality equation without a model, for each transition, and to which fixed-point equation is that learning applied the Robbins–Monroe algorithm? The algorithm is as simple as TD(0). It assigns weights to the old estimate and to the single-sample estimate on the right-hand side of the Bellman equation. The weight of understanding is placed in three places: (i) why rather than , (ii) why the action can be chosen with any policy (off-policy), and (iii) why search is still a problem. The convergence theorem is treated at the level of results and proof ideas.

3 0. Starting point

3.1 Can the optimality equation be solved without a model?

First question to consider. TD(0) was obtained by replacing the expected value of the policy evaluation equation with a single sample. What happens if we apply the same operation to the optimality equation ? And even if we obtain , what is required again when selecting a policy?

Answer. The problem to be solved

and the optimization target is policy. What is desired is a model-free variant of VI·PI. has two stumbling blocks.

  1. max is outside the expected value. . With a single sample, it is impossible to create a bias-free “max value by comparing the expected values for each action” → Section 4.2.2
  2. The model is needed again for policy extraction. → Section 5.3.1

Solving the two problems at once is learning the state-action value function . In the Bellman equation of , the max falls inside the expectation value, and policy extraction is performed without a model as .

TipSignificance

Q-learning is the first and most representative of the RL algorithms we will see, and it is the foundation of many algorithms such as DQN. However, there are almost no new ideas. It is simply the application of the TD operation of “writing the Bellman equation in the form of expectations and converting expectations into samples” to the equation . What is new is the choice of what to apply it to.

4 I. Q-function and its Bellman equation

4.1 What is

First question to consider. is the “expected cumulative reward when doing one’s best, starting from state ”. If we group the first action into , what is the quantity? What if we maximize that with respect to ?

Answer. The optimal Q-function is the maximum expected cumulative reward that can be obtained starting from state and fixing the first action to .

The argument is not a single state, but a (state, action) pair. Policy determines only the action of , and is enforced. Directly from the definition

Maximizing the optimal value with respect to the first action again results in the optimal value free up to the first action → Section 4.2.1

5.4 Off-policy

First question to consider. Must the policy for selecting action in Step 2 be the same as the policy targeted by learning (greedy for )?

Answer. It does not have to be the same. Q-learning learns properly regardless of the policy used to generate behavior. This is called an off-policy algorithm.

What goes into the target value is not the actual next action to be taken, but , that is, the selection of the optimal policy, which is the learning goal. Therefore, the policy that generates the action does not appear in the target value.

Result:

  • It has very high flexibility. You can choose any behavior, such as greedy, ε-greedy, or Boltzmann.
  • Already collected samples can be reused to update. Experience replay utilizes this property when scaling to larger problems (DQN), and it improves sample efficiency.

6.1 Problems with Greedy policies

First question to consider. If we only use greedy actions on the current during training, which cells remain unupdated? If there are unupdated cells, which assumption of the Convergence Theorem is violated?

Answer. The Greedy policy chooses the action that appears most beneficial at the current (exploitation).

If is optimal, then the greedy policy is optimal. However, the probability that is near the optimal value early in training is very low.

The problem is search. If only a greedy policy is used, some state-action pairs may never be visited. In that case, the information for those cells can never be obtained, and convergence to the optimal Q-factor is not guaranteed. Even if all states are visited, certain beneficial actions may never be attempted.

6.1.2 Exploitation–exploration trade-off

Answer.

  • To obtain a near-optimal policy with Q-learning, we must explore all potentially beneficial state-action pairs to gather information.
  • If a greedy policy is used for every update, certain beneficial actions may never be attempted even if all states are explored.
  • To overcome this, you must sacrifice some of the immediate gains you can obtain now through greedy choices and explore thoroughly.
  • This trade-off arises from a lack of knowledge regarding system dynamics and compensation structures. To acquire that knowledge, one must search instead of focusing on current gains.
TipSignificance

If the model is known, no search is needed. The VI calculates every every time. The search problem is the price paid for being model-free, and it arises in all sequential decision problems where the model is unknown, not limited to RL. This problem will be addressed again later using methods such as entropy normalization.

6.2 ε-greedy and other methods

First question to think of. How can you make all actions continuously attempted by slightly modifying a greedy policy?

Answer.

ε-greedy. Choose a greedy action with probability and a random action with probability . In other words, search for a probability of .

Another method:

  • Segment Switching. (i) Alternate between search segments and (ii) greedy segments. Use random actions in search segments and greedy actions in greedy segments.
  • Boltzmann Search. Probability of action from state Select . is the temperature parameter → Section 6.2.2

ε-greedy is the most widely used in Q-learning. This is not because it is efficient, but because it is simple and allows scheduling of ε.

NoteRationale: ε-greedy attempts all actions infinitely in a visited state.

Let us assume that a state is visited infinitely often. At each visit, the conditional probability that each action is selected, regardless of the past, is at least . Since the sum of conditional probabilities diverges (a conditional version of the Borel–Cantelli lemma), each action is selected infinitely with a probability of 1.

However, this is the case if states are visited infinitely. Whether all states are visited infinitely depends on the connection structure of the MDP.

↓ Down: Section 6.2.1 · Section 6.2.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

6.2.1 ε scheduling

First question to consider. How does the quality of differ between the early and late stages of training? Should one start with a large ε or a small ε?

Answer. Start with a large ε and gradually decrease.

  • Initial: Since there is almost no known information, focus on searching to improve the quality of .
  • Review: If becomes reliable, reduce ε and use greedy behavior more.

ε can also be fixed from beginning to end.

NoteReason: If you reduce too quickly

There is a tension in the rate at which ε is reduced, similar to the SA step size, which dictates that it “should be reduced, but not too quickly.” If the search probability at the -th visit of a certain state is , then is required for an infinite search. For example, is sufficient, but allows for only a finite number of searches with a probability of 1 (Borel–Cantelli). The goal of schedule design is to ensure that the search continues infinitely while eventually approaching greediness.

TipSignificance

It is the principle that “the more information is accumulated, the more one trusts their own estimate.” It is a design in the same direction as starting with a large λ in TD(λ) and reducing it.

7.1.2 What organization means in reality

Answer. It is sufficient to know the fact that there is a theoretical guarantee and its structure (reduction + noise conditions). Even when running tabular Q-learning on simple problems, it is very difficult to perfectly learn .

  • The core assumption of “visiting all state-action pairs infinitely” cannot be satisfied in reality.

2 Entire Tree

  • 0. Starting Point: RL is the problem of goal-oriented agents interacting with uncertain environments → Section 3.1
    • Data → Information → Decision Making → Section 3.1.1
  • I. Combined with two roots

      • Curse of Dimensions as a Number → Section 4.1.1

  • VI. Cleanup → Section 9.1

3 0. Starting point

3.1 What kind of problem is reinforcement learning?

A question to consider first. In the MDPs discussed so far, and were given. What does the agent exchange with the environment, and what does it gain from that exchange?

Answer. Reinforcement learning is the problem of goal-oriented agents interacting with an uncertain environment. The agent sends out an action (decision), and the environment returns the next state and a reward (feedback). Through this interaction, the agent learns about the environment while simultaneously learning a better policy. In other words

TipSignificance
  • “Goal-oriented” means that there is an objective function (expected cumulative reward). This is the root of optimal control → Section 4.1
  • “Adaptation through interaction” is rooted in trial-and-error learning → Section 4.2
  • Most model-free methods do not explicitly estimate the environment’s model in interactions. They directly update values or policies → Section 8.1

↓ Scroll Down: Section 3.1.1

3.1.1 If intelligent systems are viewed as Data → Information → Decision Making, what role does RL play?

Answer. Taking autonomous vehicles as an example, intelligence can be divided into two stages.

Usually, the two parts are designed separately, but RL can be an algorithm that learns end-to-end from data to decision-making. Such a system must adapt to uncertainties such as other vehicles and people, weather, road construction, and passengers.

↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

4 I. Combine with two roots

4.1 What does optimal control solve, and where does DP get stuck?

First question to consider. When applying VI·PI earlier, (i) what did you absolutely have to know, and (ii) what was the amount of computation proportional to?

Answer. Optimal control is the problem of designing a controller that maximizes the performance of a dynamic system over an entire time interval (finite or infinite). The key point is that the objective is the performance of the entire interval, not the performance at a single point in time. Although Bellman’s dynamic programming in the 1950s laid the foundation for this problem, DP has two limitations.

  1. Model Knowledge: You must fully understand (and ) to apply the Bellman operator → Section 4.1.2
  2. Scalability: State space grows exponentially with respect to dimension (curse of dimension) → Section 4.1.1

RL is an attempt to solve these two problems of (stochastic) optimal control. It can be used without a model and finds a tractable approximate solution instead of the exact optimal solution.

TipSignificance: The goal determines the year

In the path problem from a starting point to a destination, if the goal is time reduction, one path becomes optimal, and if the goal is fuel minimization, the other path becomes optimal. In optimal control, “optimal” is meaningful only with respect to the objective function. This is the same reason why the reward design determines the outcome policy in RL.

↓ Down: Section 4.1.1 · Section 4.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

4.1.1 If you write the Curse of Dimensions as a number

First question to consider. If the state consists of components and each component is discretized into steps, what is ? VI What is the cost of one step?

Answer.

NoteBasis
  • VI 1 time: Calculate for all . Since is the sum of , each term, .
  • Number of Policies: Since one action is chosen independently for each state, . As MDP theory has shown that deterministic stationary policies are sufficient, the search space is finite, but its size is an exponent of .
  • Example: If and , then . Just storing requires elements.
TipSignificance

As long as or are treated exactly as a tabular, this cost cannot be avoided. Therefore, RL abandons exact solutions from the outset and reduces the representation using functional approximations (linear features, neural networks). The price for this is the difficulty of “limited representation” → Section 7.1.2

↑ Go Up: Section 4.1

4.1.2 Where is model dependency hidden in VI·PI?

Answer. There are three places.

TipSignificance
  • The enhancement step of PI becomes when is used, and the model disappears. What remains is “how to calculate the expected value without the model”.
  • The answer to this question is the next topic, stochastic approximation. We replace the expectation with the sample and gradually reduce the step size so that the noise in the sample disappears over time.

↑ Go Up: Section 4.1

4.2 What does trial and error learning mean?

Answer. It has roots in psychology.

  • Thorndike (1911), Law of Effect: Among various responses to the same situation, responses accompanied by satisfaction have a stronger connection to the situation and appear more frequently when the situation arises again, while responses accompanied by discomfort have a weaker connection and appear less frequently.
  • Klopf (1972): Connected this idea to trial-and-error learning and related it to vast experimental data in animal learning psychology.
  • Sutton & Barto (1970–80s): Temporal-Difference (TD) learning is the algorithm developed from this.
TipSignificance: If you interpret the law of effect as a probabilistic policy

The statement “responses accompanied by satisfaction appear more readily” can be interpreted as an update that increases the probability of actions with higher rewards in a stochastic policy . This aligns with the intuition of policy gradient. On the other hand, if interpreted as storing and updating the “strength of the connection between situation and response” numerically, it aligns with the intuition of the value-based method that updates → Section 8.1

↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

4.3 What becomes of two roots when combined

Answer. If written in one line

The representative algorithm family is as follows.

Series Representative Year
value-based Q-learning (Watkins) 1989
policy-based policy gradient (Williams; Marbach & Tsitsiklis) 1987; 1998
Combination of the two actor-critic (Witten, Barto, Sutton, Degris, White, etc.) —
TipSignificance
  • Until around 2010, applications were limited to games like Tetris and chess, and some robotics, mostly remaining at the toy level. The main reason was the limitations of expression.
  • Since the 2010s, with the advancement of deep learning and computational resources, deep RL, which expresses values and policies using neural networks, has expanded to practical problems.

↓ Down: Section 8.1 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

5 II. Five Characteristics of RL

5.1 What is the difference between RL and supervised learning?

Answer.

  1. No supervisor and only reward signals → Section 5.1.1
  2. Feedback is not immediate and is delayed → Section 5.1.2
  3. Time is important. It is a sequential decision and the data is not iid → Section 5.1.2
  4. Agent’s behavior affects data to be received later → Section 5.1.3
  5. There is a trade-off between exploration and exploitation → Section 5.1.4
TipSignificance

4 is the most fundamental. In supervised learning, the data distribution is fixed regardless of the learner. In RL, if the learner changes the policy, the data distribution changes. 5 is a direct consequence of 4. Since the learner must decide for themselves which data to look at, they must choose between an action that looks good now and an action that provides more information.

↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

5.1.1 ✍ Why Rewards Cannot Serve as Correct Answer Labels

Guide Question:

  1. What do we need to know to provide the “correct action” as the label for supervised learning in the state ? If we write it as ?
  2. What is the difference between and ? Does always hold?
  3. If , then it is . In that case, is RL supervised learning?
NoteSolution

1. The correct action is . In other words, to be the label, you must know the long-term gain .

2. This difference depends on (since the action changes the distribution of the next state). Therefore, the argmax of immediate reward and the argmax of long-term gain are generally different. A counterexample is found in Section 6.1.1’s example. Reward is not the correct label because it measures only immediate gain.

3. No. If it is , the lag problem disappears, but only the reward for a single selected action is observed. Since the reward for unselected actions is not visible, “which action was the correct answer” is still not given (bandit feedback). In supervised learning, the correct answer is given for every input, but here, only the score for the chosen action is given. Therefore, even if it is , the search problem (Section 5.1.4) remains.

TipSignificance

There are two reasons why rewards cannot serve as supervised learning labels: (i) temporal: rewards do not reflect long-term gains (when ). (ii) counterfactual: the consequences of uneven behavior are not observed (even when ). RL algorithms treat (i) as the Bellman equation and (ii) as search.

↑ Go Up: Section 5.1

5.1.2 Why is feedback delayed, and why is the data not iid?

First question to consider. When following a stationary policy , write the state distribution at time in terms of the initial distribution and transition.

Answer. , if we let the state distribution be the row vector ,

  • Not iid: is not independent because it depends on , and it is not identically distributed because varies according to .
  • Feedback is delayed: Action changes the distribution of , and this propagates to . The result of appears not just in , but across the entire subsequent reward system. The current choice changes the very paths that can be taken later.
TipSignificance
  • The convergence logic of supervised learning (iid sample mean) cannot be used as is. This is why a “conditional” mean condition (conditional on past history ) is applied to the noise in subsequent convergence analysis.
  • Reducing inter-sample correlations with experience replay in deep RL also targets the same problem.

↑ Go Up: Section 5.1

5.1.3 What exactly does it mean that behavior changes the data distribution?

Answer. In the equation Section 5.1.2, the distribution of data is a function of the policy through Z and . If the policy changes to during training, the distribution of the next collected data also changes.

TipSignificance
  • Supervised learning: Fixed data distribution → Model training. It is one-way.
  • RL: Policy → Data Distribution → Policy Update → Data Distribution … There is a feedback loop.

In an unfamiliar environment, whether to choose the path that seems best based on the information (or belief) currently available, or to choose an action that provides more information because one knows less, depends on the situation. There is generally no known method to optimally balance these two → Section 5.1.4

↑ Go Up: Section 5.1

5.1.4 Why does the search-utilization trade-off occur, and what goes wrong without search

First question to consider. If we always choose the greedy action for the current estimate , what happens to the estimate of the action that was once underestimated?

Answer. It is not updated. This is because new data does not arrive due to unevenness. Therefore, if the initial estimate is unfortunately wrong, it can remain in the suboptimal state forever.

NoteExample: Case where greedy fails with a probability of 0.3 or higher

Two actions, one state (bandit that is ).

  • Action A: The reward is always .
  • Action B: The rewards are with probabilities and with probabilities . Since the expected value is , B is optimal.

Try each action once, use the sample mean as the estimate, and then choose greedy.

  • If B’s first reward is (probability ), then . After that, always choose A, A’s estimate remains , and B is not tried again. It stays on A forever.
  • Even if B’s first reward is , the same thing happens if B’s sample mean unfortunately drops below afterwards.

Therefore, the probability of failure is at least . It does not decrease no matter how long data is collected.

TipSignificance
  • The cause of the trade-off is that the environment model (, ) is unknown. If the model were known, there would be no reason to search. Therefore, this is not a problem unique to RL, but a problem in all sequential decision-making problems where the model is unknown.
  • Choosing an action that provides more information, even if it means sacrificing a small immediate gain (greedy), can be advantageous in the long run. The simplest implementation is -greedy ( probability greedy, probability random).
  • The Q-learning convergence theorem assumes that “all are visited infinitely often” to exclude the failure shown in this example.

↑ Go Up: Section 5.1

6 III. Formalization

6.1 What are the components and policies of an RL problem?

Answer.

  • State : State of the environment (system).
  • Action : Determined by the agent and affects the state.
  • Reward : Evaluates the benefits of the state and action.
  • Policy : A transition from state to action. It is the subject of optimization.

The goal of sequential decision-making is to select actions over time to maximize the expected cumulative reward.

TipSignificance: Why use probabilistic policies

Since the optimal policy of an MDP exists among deterministic and stationary policies, a stochastic policy is not necessary in terms of optimality alone. However, stochastic policies are useful in RL algorithms.

  • Search can be put into the policy itself(-greedy, Boltzmann) → Section 5.1.4
  • Since is differentiable with respect to , we can use the policy gradient. The argmax of the deterministic policy is not differentiable → Section 8.1

↓ Down: Section 6.1.1 · Section 6.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

TipSignificance

↑ Go Up: Section 6.1

6.1.2 Why are MDP problems difficult to solve?

First question to consider. Look at the decision variable, the calculation of the objective function, and the size of the search space, respectively.

Answer. It is triple-layered difficult.

  1. The decision variable is a function. The optimization target is not a number but a policy, that is, a (or ) event. Even when narrowed down to deterministic stationary policies, there are candidates → Section 4.1.1
  2. A model is required even to calculate a single objective function. The value of a single policy, , is the expected value of the trajectory distribution over an infinite number of time points, and that distribution is defined as and . To calculate this, must be solved, and is input into it → Section 4.1.2
  3. Scale. Even when solved exactly, the cost is a polynomial with respect to , and itself is exponential with respect to the state dimension.
TipSignificance

MDP theory solved the difficulty of 1 using the Bellman equation and contraction mapping. Instead of directly exploring the policy space, it found fixed points in the value space. What remains are 2 (model) and 3 (scale), which are exactly the two limits of DP. RL treats 2 as samples and 3 as approximations.

↑ Go Up: Section 6.1

7 IV. RL Problem

7.1 What is an RL problem, and how is it approached?

Answer.

  • Objective: Solve the MDP problem Section 6.1.2 when model is unknown.
  • Approach: Trial and error. The agent accumulates experience (data) through actions and gradually updates values or policies using that data. The basic unit of data is the transition sample .

↓ Down: Section 7.1.1 · Section 7.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

7.1.1 What is assumed not to be known

Answer. In most cases, it is assumed that only is unknown. Since the reward function is designed by the user, it is often known.

However, mathematically, it is possible to handle cases where even is unknown. It can be viewed as a black box (e.g., expert scoring) where inputting yields only the signal , and it can be assumed that the signal is contaminated with noise.

NoteReasoning: Why noisy compensation does not change the problem

The objective function is the expected value. Noise with a conditional mean of disappears due to the tower property (assuming the reward is bounded and allows for an exchange between the sum and the expectation). Therefore, the optimal policy is the same. Noise only slows down learning and does not change the goal.

↑ Go Up: Section 7.1

7.1.2 Why RL is useful and why it is difficult

Answer.

Useful reason Difficult reason
Flexibility: Can be used without model information Limited Knowledge: No model information
Adaptability: Since it does not rely on a fixed model, it can continue to update even if the environment changes Exploration vs. Exploitation: It is unclear what to try → Section 5.1.4
Extensibility: Can be used for large-scale problems because it abandons exact solutions from the start and obtains tractable approximate solutions Bound Representation: It is unclear in what functional form the values and policies of complex problems should be approximated
TipSignificance: Each row of the table is a two-sided representation of the same property.
  • The fact that “there is no model” becomes flexibility on the first line and limited knowledge on the right. It is a double-edged sword.
  • Line 2: Since it does not rely on a fixed model, it can adapt, but that is precisely why you have to decide for yourself what to try.
  • Line 3: Since we chose an approximation, it can be used for large-scale problems, but if the form of the approximation is chosen incorrectly, it cannot even come close to the optimal.

↑ Go Up: Section 7.1

8 V. Algorithm Classification

8.1 What criteria do RL algorithms use for division?

First question to consider. Is the object that the algorithm learns and holds (a) only the value function, (b) only the policy, or (c) both?

Answer. Divide into the relationship between two circles: the set using the value function and the set using the policy.

Classification Training Target Method of obtaining policy Representative

policy-based policy only () directly parameterize policy policy gradient
actor-critic Both evaluate actor() as critic(value) and update actor-critic

TipSignificance
  • The subsequent order is value-based (stochastic approximation → TD → Q-learning) → policy-based (policy gradient) → actor-critic.
  • Apart from this classification, there is a model-based / model-free axis. Most model-free methods do not explicitly estimate but directly update values or policies.
  • The reason why probabilistic policies are essential in policy-based systems lies in the significance of Section 6.1.

↑ Go Up: Section 4.3

3.1 Can the fixed-point problem be solved model-free?

First question to consider. Where exactly was the transition probability used at each step of VI and PI? If you do not know Z and can only obtain the transition sample , what can be used to replace it?

Answer. VI and PI are both methods for solving the fixed-point problem. And the model is placed in the expected value position, , inside the Bellman operator. The expected value can be approximated by samples. However, a single sample can differ significantly from the expected value. Therefore, stochastic approximation (SA) is designed so that this error (noise) is averaged out and disappears through iteration.

TipSignificance

SA is the theoretical framework for value-based RL algorithms (TD, Q-learning). Subsequently, Q-learning is derived as “applying Robbins–Monroe SA to the Bellman equation for ” → Section 5.1.2

4.2.1 Reasons why noise can disappear over time

Answer. If the update equation is written by separating it into the movement direction and noise, it is as follows.

When accumulated up to the step , the contribution of noise is in the form . If the conditional mean of the noise is 0, this sum is a martingale. On the other hand, the contribution in the average direction continues to accumulate in proportion to . Eventually, the noise is averaged out and disappears, and the trajectory follows a deterministic iteration.

3 0. Starting point

3.1 Can the value of a policy be obtained online without a model?

First question to consider. Where are transition probabilities used when iteratively solving the policy evaluation equation ? What form should the equation take to adjust the estimate every time a transition sample is received?

Answer. The problem to be solved is the two fixed-point problem.

The root of the two equations is the same value decomposition. It divides value into immediate rewards and cumulative rewards obtained by following the policy from the next state. VI·PI was created based on the fact that and are abbreviations, but was required every time the operator was applied.

Here, we begin by covering policy evaluation. We classify the methods based on two criteria.

Method model-free (does not use ) online (updates for every transition)

TipSignificance

All TD series originate from the same operation: “writing the value decomposition in the form of expectations and converting those expectations into samples.” MC, TD(0), and TD(λ) differ depending on what is converted into samples (the entire trajectory, a single step, or a weighted average of multiple steps). For the optimality equation side, applying the same operation to results in Q-learning.

Answer. Weight the old estimate and the single-sample version of the new estimate .

If you group it as , the at the beginning and end will be erased.

TD(λ) Algorithm

This is also a policy evaluation method, and only one element is updated in each iteration. Since ’s is required for the update, it is not completely online unless TD(0) is collected, so it can be updated after collecting some trajectory data.

↓ Down: Section 6.3.1 · Section 6.3.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

6.3.1 ✍ Two extremes: λ = 0 and λ = 1

Guide Question:

  2. If , , then what is ? Assume .
NoteSolution

1. If we use the convention , is 1 and is 0. Only remains in the sum. TD(0)

2. It becomes a telephoto lens. Therefore, the updates are and . This is the same form as the Monte Carlo iteration of Section 4.1. All intermediate values are eliminated, and only the actual reward remains.

TipSignificance

TD(λ) is a continuous family with TD(0) and MC as the endpoints. λ controls how much to bootstrap on the current estimate and how far to use the actual reward → Section 7.1

↑ Go Up: Section 6.3

6.3.2 What is the “0” of TD(0)?

Answer. This means that 0 is entered for the parameter λ of TD(λ). If λ = 0, all weights of Section 6.2 are concentrated in the 1-step equation ().

“0” is not the number of steps being looked ahead. TD(0) is a 1-step method that observes one reward and writes the value of the state one step later. In n-step TD notation where the number of steps is specified directly, TD(0) corresponds to 1-step TD.

↑ Go Up: Section 6.3

7 IV. Selection of λ

7.1 Bias–variance trade-off

First question to consider. Given the target value of TD(0) and the target value of MC , where does the bias come from and where does the variance come from?

Answer.

  • A large λ is close to MC. MC uses only actual rewards, so it is unbiased. However, since it sums up both random rewards and transitions from long trajectories, it has large variance.
  • Small λ is close to TD(0). Since it approximates a single sample with the current estimate , the bias is large while is inaccurate. Instead, the variance is small because there is only one step of random elements.
NoteRationale: Comparison of target values

The update of TD(λ) is to move toward the next target value.

  • : , that is, the actual discount accumulation reward. Random terms are accumulated for the length of the trajectory.
  • : . There is only one random term, . Instead, the error of is incorporated directly into the target value.

↓ Down: Section 7.1.1 · Section 7.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

7.1.1 ✍ Two-state example

In a Markov chain, two states 1 and 2 are adjacent, and . Each locus visits state 1 exactly once.

NoteSolution

1. Since it is visited only once, is by definition an independent sample of Z and (ignoring truncation). Writing the sample mean corresponds to TD(1).

2. Cannot be used. The target value of TD(1) is only the sum of actual rewards, and does not include any state value estimates → Section 6.3.1

3. Let be the reward for a 1→2 transition.

  • TD(0): . Randomness is only (0 if the reward is deterministic like the model in this note).
  • MC: . Due to Markov properties, the future after state 2 is independent of , so

TD(0) eliminates variance of . This is because the noise of the entire future starting from state 2 has been replaced by a single accurate estimate.

TipSignificance

TD(0) utilizes already learned value information very efficiently and also reduces noise in the reward samples. However, that efficiency is only when is accurate. If is incorrect, that error is transferred directly to . This is the price of bias.

↑ Go Up: Section 7.1

7.1.2 λ scheduling

First question to consider. How does the quality of differ between the early and late stages of learning? Accordingly, which error should be a greater concern?

Answer. Start with a large λ and reduce to 0.

  • Initial: Since the quality of is poor, relying on results in a large bias. Reduce the bias by using a large λ to apply more real rewards.
  • Review: Since TD(λ) converges, the quality of improves as the process progresses. Now, relying on also results in small bias. By utilizing existing value information with a small λ, we reduce variance and update quickly.
TipSignificance

It is the principle that “the more reliable information accumulates, the more it relies on its own estimate.” It is a design in the same direction as the ε schedule, which starts with a large search probability and reduces it.

↑ Go Up: Section 7.1

8 V. Convergence

8.1 Convergence Theorem

Answer.

ImportantTheorem (Convergence of TD(λ))

In practice, satisfying the “visiting every state infinitely often” and step size conditions is very tricky. Remember the fact that theoretical guarantees exist and the structure in which they stem from the two axes of SA (contraction + noise conditions).

item.title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
item.description:
1 View entire flow at a glance

Steps Key Questions Key Tools
Policy Evaluation How to calculate the performance of a given ? Vector form, inverse matrix, operator , γ-contraction, Banach
Optimum Value How is characterized and calculated? Bellman Operator , Concomitantness/Monotonicity, Value Iteration
Optimal Policy Does an Optimal Policy Exist? How Is It Created? Argmax Configuration, Fixed Point Identification
Policy iteration Can policy space information be used? Monotonic enhancement, Monotonic convergence theorem

Order of proof: (1) Formulate the policy evaluation equation → (2) Show the uniqueness of the solution using contractility and fixed points → (3) Show the optimality of Bellman fixed points → (4) Prove the monotonicity of Policy Improvement → (5) Prove why the limit is optimal. The important thing is not memorizing the formulas, but the reasons justifying each equality and inequality.

The roots of all proofs eventually converge on two facts.

ImportantThe root of all proofs
  1. The weighted average cannot exceed the maximum value. Since each row of and are probability distributions, the multiplication operation between them is a weighted average.
  2. shrinks the error. The error that did not increase by the average is multiplied by and actually reduced.

2 Review: Finite-horizon DP

2.1 Discrete State·Behavior

After initializing , perform backward induction on .

  • Find the optimal value function and the optimal policy at each time point exactly.
  • There can be multiple optimal policies. This is because there can be multiple argmaxes.
  • Hidden Complexity: For every state, there is a behavior maximization for every operation. If the state and behavior space is large, it does not scale up.

2.2 Extension to continuous control

About ,

  • Use sup instead of max. An optimal policy may not exist (find the optimal policy only when a maximizer exists).
  • Action maximization is difficult, and since it cannot be evaluated across the entire continuous state space, discretization is involved, leading to scalability issues.

3 Infinite-horizon discounted MDP

3.1 Definition

NoteDefinition (Discounted MDP)

tuple

  • : State set, : Behavior set
  • : Probability that the next state is when the current state is and the current action is .
  • : Scalar reward function measuring the gain of the current state/action
  • : Discount rate determining how much future rewards will be discounted

3.2 Assumption

  1. Stationary reward and transition probability: and do not change over time.
    • In the finite horizon, the reward could be time-dependent, and the transition probability could also be set to be time-dependent.
    • In the infinite horizon, the function itself does not directly depend on time.
  2. Finite set of states and actions: . Since the combinations are finite, the rewards are bounded. That is, for some constant , , .
  3. Discount: .

3.3 Result: Cumulative rewards are always boundless

By combining finite states and actions with discounting, any value falls within the same upper bound. It is a neat setup where there is no need to worry about the divergence of cumulative rewards.

4 Value function and stationary policy

4.1 Value function

NoteDefinition (Value function)

Expected value of cumulative reward when using policy starting from state .

  • Practice until this meaning comes to mind automatically. Intuitive understanding is much more important than mathematical definition.
  • The starting point is irrelevant. Since we add up to infinity and shift the discount weight by the starting point, the value is the same regardless of what is.
  • If the value function is calculated, the policy evaluation is completed by simply inserting the initial state into the state position.

4.2 Stationary Policy

Generally, the policy is . is the decision rule written at time , i.e., the state → action transition. In the finite horizon, different optimal decision rules actually emerged at each time step.

A policy being stationary means that the same decision rule is used at every point in time.

Since there is no need to distinguish between decision rules and policies, write it simply as follows.

  • Deterministic stationary:
  • Stochastic stationary: (Probability distribution of actions by state)
TipQ) If it is a stationary policy, does it perform the same action at every point in time?

No. Although the event is fixed, the input (state) changes at every time step, so the output (action) also changes. Most reinforcement learning algorithms assume a stationary policy. The fact that considering only a stationary policy is sufficient is justified by the existence of an optimal policy].

5 Policy Evaluation: Decomposition of the Value Function

5.1 Bellman expectation equation

Decompose the value function into (i) immediate reward and (ii) discounted next state value.

Since actions are involved in both rewards and transition probabilities, randomized policies take the expected value of actions as the outer sum.

5.2 Proof (tower rule)

  • Line 1: Separate the infinite sum into the point term and the term thereafter.
  • Row 2: Apply conditional expectation to one more time (tower rule)
  • Line 3: By definition, the inner part is a value function with an initial state of (thanks to stationarity)
  • Row 4: The distribution of is a weighted sum of the distributions of and with transition probabilities

Why use conditional expectation twice? Instead of calculating the total probability all at once, we calculate the expected reward by assuming the next state is determined first, and then take the average over the uncertainty of itself. This is the intuition behind the tower rule . Here, the fact that future rewards can be expressed as a function is due to Markov properties and a time-independent stationary policy.

TipVerification Question: Why does remain only once in the sum?

This is because it was separated into in the future reward section. The inner sum becomes ‘starting from the next state’, leaving only one for starting one step late.

5.3 What is different from Finite Horizon?

  • There is no concept of time. Since stationary compensation and transitions are assumed, the equation is the same at every time point. The influence of time is hidden within the definition of the value function.
  • Therefore, the calculation method changes. In the finite horizon, since the left side is the value at time and the right side is , it was possible to calculate one by one backward from the terminal condition. In the infinite horizon, since the same function exists on both the left and right sides, it is impossible to calculate starting from the terminal point. → A method to “solve” the equation is required.

6 Vector form

If labeled as , , it can be written as follows.

Value Vector Original state → value mapping, but since can have values, the outputs are listed and viewed as a dimensional vector.

Expected Reward Vector The element at is the expected reward value when using policy in state . If deterministic, it is .

Transition Probability Matrix The element represents the probability that the next state is when policy is applied from state . If deterministic, it is .

Vector Equation equations are written in a single line, and calculating each element yields exactly the same as the previous equation.

Important is row-stochastic

and Therefore, and . Almost all proofs in this text start from this fact.

7 Existence and Uniqueness of Solutions and Inverse Matrix Representation

Since the vector equation is linear, if we simplify it The fact that a unique solution exists is equivalent to being reversible.

7.1 (A) Reason why the eigenvalue is 1 or less

The eigenvalue is “how many times it becomes when multiplied,” so it is .

Since eigenvalues can be complex numbers, the exact proposition is .

7.6 Why Inverse Matrices Are Not Often Used

The problem of interest usually has a very large number of states.

  • Operational amount: Solving linear systems
  • Memory: stores . If , then elements

→ We need a precise method rather than an approximation, but one that avoids the inverse matrix. This is the operator form and fixed-point iteration.

8 Operator Forms and Fixed Point Problems

The policy evaluation equation is becomes a fixed point problem.

  • I have only rewritten the derived equation, and I have not yet explained how to solve it.
  • Since exists on both the left and right sides, this is the perspective of viewing the entire right side as the output obtained by applying the mapping to .
  • This formulation is the idea that forms the basis of value-based RL.
TipLet’s distinguish between and
  • is the result of a one-step update, assuming the current step follows policy and the value after the next state is input .
  • is the actual expected cumulative reward when the policy is used infinitely from the beginning.
  • Therefore, for any , it cannot be said that . holds only when .

This distinction is key to not confusing the following (one new action + future value of existing policy) with policy evaluation .

9 Contraction Properties and Banach Fixed Point Theorem

9.1 Definition

NoteDefinition (γ-contraction)

The fact that the ||| operator is a γ-contraction with respect to is

Intuition: The distance between any two points after passing them through an operator is reduced to times less than before. This contractility plays a very important role in reinforcement learning.

9.2 is γ-contraction

Noteproposition

is a γ-contraction with respect to for any stationary policy .

9.2.1 Intuition: The error is reduced through three steps

What does is “my reward + γ × (average of next state values)”. We only need to track the difference (error between the two estimates .

Step What happens Effect on error
① Add reward Added equally to both Canceled out, no effect
② Average as Probability-weighted average of the next state values Since the average cannot exceed the maximum value, it does not increase
③ Multiply by Reduced by a factor of γ

9.2.2 Induction

Step 1. The reward disappears.

Step 2. Look only at one state . is the weighted average of .

Step 3. The average cannot exceed the maximum value.

Step 4. Attach γ and max for .

It is one line in matrix norms: .

9.2.4 Supplement

  • Why sup-norm: is the error of the state with the largest error, and the probability mean cannot increase the largest error. The norm for which holds is the -norm. In the general , can exceed 1, so the reduction is not guaranteed.
  • Constant γ is tight: If , then , so equality holds.

9.3 Banach Fixed Point Theorem

NoteBanach fixed point theorem

If is a contraction concept

  1. has the unique fixed point ().
  2. Starting from an arbitrary and defined as , then .

( is a fully equipped street space.)

Convergence Rate: If the fixed point is , With each iteration, the distance from the fixed point decreases by a factor of γ, and converges exponentially regardless of where it starts.

Direct Proof of Uniqueness: If there are two fixed points, then , so .

TipQ) Why is uniqueness important?

If there are multiple fixed points, when a fixed point is reached through iteration, it is impossible to know if it is the true that was intended. Thanks to uniqueness, as long as convergence is achieved, it is guaranteed that the convergence point is . This is important not only theoretically but also practically.

Reasons why the fixed point can be called : (1) Since the Bellman expectation equation was derived from the definition of cumulative reward, is actually the fixed point. (2) By Banach’s theorem, that fixed point is unique. Therefore, the fixed point found through iteration is not another candidate, but exactly **.

Conclusion: The policy evaluation equation has a unique solution, and can be obtained through fixed-point iteration.

9.4 Value iteration for policy evaluation

Notealgorithm
  • Input: stationary policy
  • Initialization: Random (if continuous, a random function)
  • Repeat until convergence:

Hidden Complexity: Although written concisely in operator form, in reality, one iteration is completed only after updating all states. If it is a Deterministic policy However, there is no action maximization. This is because the action is fixed as . Action maximization is added when calculating the optimal value.

10 Optimum Value Function and Bellman Operator

10.1 Optimum value function

The goal is to solve the following problem.

NoteDefinition (Optimal value function)

The maximum expected value of cumulative rewards obtainable from the starting state . Since it is an infinite horizon, the starting point does not matter.

10.2 Bellman operator

Maximize the sum of the immediate reward and the expected cumulative reward from the next state, in accordance with the idea of dynamic programming.

Notedefinition (Bellman operator)

This can be rewritten as follows.

(In some notations, the Bellman operator is written as . They are the same operator.)

10.3 Q) Why is the maximum for policy the same as the maximum for action?

If we let , then is the weighted average of . What needs to be proven is

(≤) The average cannot exceed the maximum value. For any , since No policy can be found that gives a value greater than the maximum for the action.

(≥) A policy exists that achieves the upper bound. If we use the Dirac distribution which concentrates the probability mass on ,

The Bellman operator is typically defined and written in a form that maximizes the action , and most literature follows this convention.

10.3.1 Meaning of vector max

is read as componentwise max.

  • The -th element depends only on . A policy is a collection of distributions that can be determined independently for each state.
  • Therefore, state-specific maximizations do not interfer with each other.
  • One achieves the maximum value simultaneously in all states.

Intuition: Randomly selecting is mixing the values of each action by probability. Since mixing cannot make the result better than the best action, randomness offers no benefit from an optimization perspective. This is the root of the idea that “deterministic optimal policies exist.”

10.4 Affine vs. Nonlinear: Why Inverse Matrices Work Only in Policy Evaluation

  • Policy Evaluation Operator: . It is affine with respect to and is a linear operator in the strict sense only in the special case where the reward is . Nevertheless, it is called ‘linear’ in the sense that is a system of linear equations. Therefore, it can be solved as .
  • Optimal Bellman Operator: is generally non-linear as it involves the maximum value for the action. Therefore, cannot be directly obtained by moving to a single fixed matrix and taking the inverse.
TipThe single difference between ‘policy evaluation’ and ‘optimization’

If policy is fixed, the values of the next states are probabilistically averaged. For optimization, a max is added to select the action itself to take that average. The two operators have the same dynamic programming structure, but the meaning of the fixed point is different.

11 The Abbreviation and Monotonicity of the Bellman Operator

Noteproposition

Bellman operator is a γ-contraction with respect to . It is also monotone. (Inequalities are element-wise, entry-wise)

11.1 Proof of Abbreviation

In a method like , an additional step is added to process the max.

Auxiliary Inequality: If we take on both sides of , we get . If we swap the roles of , the opposite side also appears.

If you use this The last inequality is the weighted average argument. Take the maximum for and you’re done.

11.2 Proof of Monotonicity

If , then in each , so Taking on both sides gives .

For the same reason, is also monotonous (the elements of are ).

12 Bellman Equation: Uniqueness and Optimality of Solutions

12.1 Q1) Why does it have a unique solution?

Since is a γ-contraction, by the first property of the Banach fixed point theorem, it has a unique fixed point. Therefore, has exactly one solution.

12.2 Q2) Why is that year

Banach’s theorem states only that “there is a unique fixed point.” The key to showing that it is is the following proposition.

Noteproposition
  • if
  • if

Fact of use:

  • (F1) For all , ( is the maximum for )
  • (F2) Since the element of is , (preserving inequality direction)

12.2.1 (a)

Fix an arbitrary . as (F1). If this is substituted recursively, the direction is maintained thanks to (F2). Since , in Since this holds for all , maximizing both sides for gives .

12.2.2 (b)

The opposite direction appears in the same way as (a), but care must be taken regarding which policy is chosen. If an arbitrary is used, combining and does not determine the relationship between and . Instead, a policy that achieves is used.

If we take the greedy policy for , we get . Therefore, it is , and with iterative substitution like (a)

Visible Usage Policy

12.2.3 Conclusion

The fixed point satisfies both and simultaneously, so it is and , i.e., .

ImportantCleanup

The Bellman equation has a unique solution, and that solution corresponds to the optimal value function. This is the fundamental theorem of optimal control and reinforcement learning.

Intuition

  • Uniqueness: reduces the distance between two candidates, so if there are two solutions, the distance becomes 0 and they become the same.
  • Optimality: indicates that “even with a one-step improvement, it cannot exceed ,” meaning that is the upper bound of the achievable value. indicates that “ is the lower bound of the actually achievable value.” The point where the two meet is .

13 Value iteration

NoteAlgorithm (Value iteration)
  • Initialization: Random
  • Repeat until convergence:

Then .

  • The policy evaluation algorithm and template are the same. The only difference is that is applied instead of .
  • Hidden Complexity: For every , for all We need to solve . Compared to policy evaluation, there is additional complexity called action maximization (parallelization per state is possible).
  • Because it performs action maximization, dynamic programming works properly and converges to the optimal value.

13.1 Difference from Finite horizon

Finite horizon Infinite horizon
Start point Fixed to termination condition Can start anywhere (arbitrary )
Number of iterations Exactly times () Not predetermined, until convergence
Decision rule Varies by time point A single stationary rule

13.2 What does the number of repetitions depend on?

depends on initialization. If happens to be near , it converges in very few iterations, and if it is taken far away, many iterations are required ().

However, the shape of the optimal value function is very difficult to intuitively understand. This is one of the reasons why reinforcement learning has developed slowly. Therefore, it is usually initialized with a zero vector, an approximate estimate of the accumulated reward, or just an arbitrary vector.

14 Existence and Configuration of Optimal Policy

ImportantOrganize

If and are finite sets, an optimal policy exists, among which there is a deterministic and stationary one. Such an optimal policy is obtained as follows.

  • The part that is more powerful than determinism is that it is stationary. You can use the same decision rule every time. This theorem explains why you can focus on stationary policies in an infinite-horizon discounted configuration.
  • Construction Method: After obtaining through value iteration, the action that maximizes the sum of the immediate reward and the next state value is assigned as the policy output, just as the Bellman equation dictates. This is very similar to the Finite Horizon approach.

14.1 Proof

  • First equality (by construction): Since contains an action that maximizes what is inside the brackets, applying is equivalent to applying .
  • Second Equals: is the only fixed point of .
  • If we connect the beginning and the end, is the fixed point of . Since is also a contraction, it has a unique fixed point, which by definition is . Therefore
  • If the policy evaluation result of a policy is equal to the optimal value, then that policy is optimal.

( is the policy evaluation operator , with substituted for , and is the Bellman operator that maximizes the action. Do not confuse these two.)

14.2 Proof Method: Constructive Proof + Fixed Point Identification

“By construction”: This means that the property automatically holds because of the way it is defined. Since the property was intentionally included when constructing the object, there is no need to prove it separately. Here, “ was made into argmax” is the basis for the first equality.

  • Constructive Proof: To show that something “exists,” the object is directly constructed. Conversely, proof by contradiction or compactness arguments only demonstrate existence without physically holding the object. Since it is a constructive proof, one also obtains an algorithm stating “this is how it can be obtained.”
  • Identifying Fixed Points: Since is the unique fixed point of , if we show that a vector is the fixed point of , then that vector is .

14.3 Points to note

  1. Where finiteness is used: argmax must not be empty to form . If is finite, the max is always achieved. This corresponds exactly to the fact in continuous control that “without a maximizer, an optimal policy may not exist.”
  2. Simultaneously Optimal in All States: Since is the maximum value for each state, the optimal policy may differ for each state. This proof shows that a single is simultaneously optimal for all . This is because state-specific maximizations do not interfere with each other.
  3. Why it is not a circular argument: To create , is required, and appears to depend on a policy by definition. However, is first determined without a policy as a fixed point of , and is created on top of it.
  4. , which is the greedy policy written in (b) of the Bellman equation, is .

15 Policy iteration

15.1 Idea

Value iteration updates information only in the value space to calculate the optimal value before moving on to the policy space. The ultimate goal is the optimal policy, but can’t we also utilize information from the policy space?

Policy iteration is a method that optimally converges values and policies simultaneously by alternately utilizing information from the value space and the policy space.

15.2 algorithm

NoteAlgorithm (Policy iteration)
  • Initialization: Random deterministic stationary policy (Initialize policy, not value)
  • Repeat until convergence:
    1. Policy Evaluation: Solve the fixed-point problem to calculate
    2. Policy improvement:

The policy enhancement phase assumes that is the optimal value and adopts the action that maximizes the current reward plus the expected cumulative reward when is used as the new policy.

15.3 Comparison of computational amounts between VI and PI

Where action maximization is Iterative structure
VI Every iteration, all states
PI Policy Improvement Phase Only Evaluation (Inner Iteration) + Improvement
  • If you use fixed-point iteration for PI policy evaluation, there will be a lot of iterations inside, and you will have to do it again for every policy.
  • However, there is no action maximization in the iteration of policy evaluation. When comparing the same state updates, a single sweep of policy evaluation is usually lighter than VI. Conversely, PI has the cost of performing policy evaluation multiple times, so the overall superiority of the algorithms cannot be determined.
  • The total computational cost depends on the implementation of policy evaluation (linear system solving or iteration), the number of states and actions, and initialization; therefore, depending on the problem, it is different which approach is faster. For PI, the speed difference is significant depending on whether the initial policy is close to the optimal policy, while for VI, it depends on whether the initial value is close to the optimal value.
  • It is a strong theoretical result that both converge to the optimal value and optimal policy.

16 Monotonal Enhancement Lemma

What does it mean mathematically that “the policy improves”? Policy performance is measured by the cumulative reward expectation across all starting states.

NoteLemma (Monotonic improvement)

For all obtained from policy iteration This does not mean that ‘policies change strictly,’ but rather that expected cumulative rewards do not worsen in all states. Since values can be the same due to ties, it is , not .

16.1 First to distinguish in the proof: Current policy · New policy · Input value

is the expected value when assuming that only the first action from the current state is set to , and from the next state onwards, the existing policy is followed.

Formula Action used in the first step Standard of value after the first step
Existing Existing
New Still Existing
Maximize all Existing
Use the new forever The actual value of the new policy itself

It is important to note that the first three are a single Bellman update, and the last one is a fixed point for policy evaluation.

16.2 Step 1. Proof that ‘changing only the first step results in no loss’

(a) Policy evaluation — The value of the existing policy is the fixed point of the operator evaluating itself.

(b) Policy improvement — The new policy selects the action that maximizes . Therefore, when the input value is , the following equation holds.

(c) Definition of Bellman operator — The value of an existing action cannot exceed the maximum value among those actions.

If you connect the three above in order

Intuition: This means that rather than acting in the existing way, it cannot be a loss to take the best action based on the existing , even if only once.

WarningThe most confusing equation

is true because the new policy was chosen greedily with respect to the existing value. However, is not true for any . In particular, and must not be swapped arbitrarily.

16.3 Step 2. Extend ‘One Step Improvement’ to ‘Use New Policy Permanently’

If we set it to , , we obtained from the front.

  1. Monotonicity: Applying the same operator to results in . Repeat this process.
  2. Coordinateness: The value of continuously applying the operator of the new fixed policy goes to the unique fixed point of .
  3. Limits and Inequalities: The relationship that holds in each state also holds in the limit.

Therefore

Roles assigned by property in the proof: (i) Maximization shows that there is no loss in the first step, (ii) Monotonicity preserves the direction of the inequality even when the operator is applied multiple times, and (iii) Reducibility guarantees that the limit of the iteration is the value of the new policy.

Tip3 lines of proof framework

If you can state the basis for the first equality/inequality/equality, the rest leads to monotonicity and conciseness.

17 Convergence of Policy Iteration

The proposition to be proven is divided into two parts.

  1. Value converges: .
  2. That convergence value is the optimal value: , and the greedy policy derived from it is optimal.

Number 2 does not automatically hold true based on number 1 alone. This is because just because the value is stable does not mean it is optimal.

17.1 Monotone convergence theorem

NoteCleanup

A bounded and component-wise monotonically non-decreasing sequence of real vectors has component-wise finite limits.

Why does this hold for vectors as well? If , then it is a sequence of real numbers where each component is bounded above and monotonically non-decreasing over time. This is because the monotonic convergence theorem for real numbers can be applied to each component.

17.2 Summary: Policy iteration reaches the optimal policy

ImportantConvergence of Policy Iteration

In a discounted MDP with finite states and actions, , performing exact policy evaluation and greedy improvement causes to converge to . For a finite set of deterministically stationary policies, the optimal value is reached with finite improvements. If the existing action is maintained in case of ties and stopped upon reaching the optimal state, the policy itself also stops at the optimal policy.

17.2.1 Step 1. Compensation is bounded → Values of all policies are also bounded

Since is finite, for all , we can choose , which is . By

Meaning: No matter how the policy changes, the value cannot grow beyond a certain upper limit.

17.2.2 Step 2. Monotonic enhancement + Bounded → Converges to some

We have already proven above. Therefore, by the monotonic convergence theorem

Up to this point, we only knew of the existence of extremes, but did not verify optimality.

17.2.3 Step 3. Key Connection: Why does satisfy the Bellman optimality equation?

When policy improvement and monotonic improvement are used together, the following relationship holds.

Reason for each symbol:

  • First equal sign: Policy evaluation, is the fixed point of .
  • First : maximizes the action, so it is not smaller than the fixed policy.
  • Second equality: Policy improvement, is selected greedily with as input.
  • Second : Forward forging improvement and forging of .
  • End equal sign: Evaluation equation of the new policy.

In other words, the key inequality is

Why is this important? Both ends converge to . The middle also converges to by the Sandwich Theorem. Meanwhile, is a contraction, so it is continuous. Therefore

If you compare the two expressions

Since we previously showed that the Bellman optimality operator has exactly one fixed point, and that it is ,

This is the core logic that bridges the gap between ‘simply converged’ and ‘converged to the optimal value’.

17.2.4 Step 4. Create the actual optimal policy from the converged value

Let’s construct a greedy policy using the limit .

Because was configured like this, regarding
