Therefore, is the optimal policy.

WarningPay attention to the order of the equation chain

If you compress this step into a single line I am tempted to write it like . However, the first equation does not hold simply because Z was defined greedily. We must show before it.

Therefore, when writing strictly, in Step 3 above, first prove , and then It is safer to understand it by changing the order to . The idea is the same, but it is arranged so that the basis for each equation is already secured in the previous step.

17.3 Why does it finish in a finite number of moves? (Using a finite policy set)

The proof up to this point has demonstrated the convergence and optimality of the value sequence. We can go a step further regarding the policy iteration of a finite MDP.

  1. If the number of states is and there are at most actions per state, then there are at most deterministic stationary policies. Therefore, the number of possible vectors is also finite.
  2. takes only a finite set of values while being monotonically non-decreasing. Therefore, at some point, two continuous values become equal: .
  3. If both ends are the same in the sandwich relationship of Step 3
  4. Therefore, is already the optimal policy, and it reaches the optimal value with a finite number of exact improvements. Even if there is a tie in the optimal actions, maintaining the existing action and stopping at the optimal state guarantees the convergence (stopping) of the policy itself.

Caution: If implemented to continuously switch to a different optimal action instead of the existing one in case of a tie, oscillation between different optimal policies may occur even in the state . Therefore, strictly speaking, value convergence and policy sequence convergence must be distinguished, and tie-breaking/termination conditions must be specified when referring to the cessation of a policy sequence.

17.4 Proof 6-Line Summary

  1. Limited rewards and discounts: .

  4. Enhancement definition + operator monotonality: .
  5. sandwich + continuity: ; with fixed point uniqueness .
  6. The greedy policy for satisfies , so it is , which is the optimal policy.

18 Numerical Example: VI and PI Comparison

18.2 Value iteration ()

Since , the error decreases exponentially, but in this example, PI, which performed accurate policy evaluation, reached the optimal state with 3 policy evaluations, whereas VI converges asymptotically. However, since each policy evaluation of PI requires internal calculation, it cannot be concluded from this single example that the overall execution time of PI is faster.

19 Value iteration vs Policy iteration

Value iteration Policy iteration
Update Rating + Improvements
Usage Information Value Space Only Value Space + Policy Space
Initialization Value Policy
Maximize Action Every Iteration Only in the Policy Enhancement Phase

TipQ) Which one should I use?

There is no single correct answer. You have to try both to know for sure. There is a significant performance difference depending on how well the initialization is performed. If the VI happens to be initialized near , it converges within a few iterations, and if the PI happens to be initialized near , the PI also converges quickly. However, since the optimal value or the shape of the optimal policy cannot be known in advance, it is difficult to perform good initialization.

20 Connection with reinforcement learning algorithms

These two algorithms form the backbone of most RL algorithms.

Series Used Example Root
Value-based value only Q-learning, DQN Value iteration
Actor-critic Value + Policy actor-critic, DDPG, SAC Policy iteration
Policy-based policy only Policy gradient —
  • In actor-critic, the actor plays the role of policy improvement, and the critic plays the role of policy evaluation. Actor-critic can be viewed as a model-free version of policy iteration (although there are differences in details and techniques).
  • Here, the ‘root’ refers to a connection at the idea level. This does not mean that each algorithm is the exact same mathematical procedure as VI·PI.
TipQ) Why can’t VI or PI be applied directly to RL?

VI and PI assume that model information, specifically the transition probabilities , is perfectly known. In RL, only state and reward samples are obtained through trial and error, and the transition probabilities are not directly known. Therefore, VI was transformed into Q-learning and PI into actor-critic by changing them to a model-free approach.

item.title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
item.description:
1 Big picture

NoteOne-sentence summary

The finite interval MDP is a difficult problem that requires optimizing functions (decision rules) simultaneously, but since the terminal condition is known, the optimal value and optimal policy can be accurately obtained by solving the Bellman equations one time step at a time from the back (backward induction).

The core flow is as follows.

  1. Problem Formula:
  2. Policy Evaluation: Define the value function and decompose it into “Immediate Reward + Next State Value” → Backward Calculation
  3. Optimization: Proof that the optimal value function is a solution to the Bellman equation (Optimality Principle)
  4. Policy Construction: Bellman Proving induction that the deterministic Markov policy constructed from the argmax on the right-hand side is optimal
  5. Algorithm: Calculate and simultaneously in a single loop using DP (backward induction).
  6. Extensions and Limitations: Continuous Control → /Integral, Absence of argmax, Curse of Dimensionality → Connected to Approximation (Deep RL)

Philosophical Significance of the Bellman Equation: Optimal decision-making in the present is an action that balances the two by considering not only immediate gains but also long-term benefits to maximize their sum.

1.1 Concept Block Map

This document is structured to stack the blocks below in order. Move to the next block if you can answer the Block Check question at the end of each block. The arrow indicates that “the previous block is needed to understand this block.”

Block Stacking Preceding Block One-line Summary
B0 MDP Components, Decision Rules vs. Policies (Section 2) – Policies are bundles of time-series decision rules
B1 finite-horizon problem formulation (Section 3) B0 functions simultaneously, a difficult problem
B2 Constructing Transition Probabilities (Section 4) B0 Deriving Transition Probabilities from System Equations
B3 Value function and terminal condition (Section 5) B1 is time dependent,
B4 Optimum value function, Optimum policy, ε-optimum policy (Section 6) B3 ,
B5 Policy Evaluation Recursion and Its Proof (Section 7) B3 Immediate Reward + Value at Next Time (tower rule)
B6 Bellman Equation, Proof of Optimality Principle (Section 8) B4, B5 is a solution to the Bellman equation
B7 argmax Optimality of Deterministic Markov Policy (Section 9) B5, B6 Induction from Back
B8 Stochastic Optimum Policy (Section 10) B7 Optimum on the distribution surface over the argmax set
B9 DP algorithm (Section 11) B6, B7 and in one loop
B10 Manual calculation (Section 12) B9 Check algorithm as numbers
B11 Continuous Control Extension and the Curse of Dimensionality (Section 13) B9 , integral, absence of argmax, limit of discretization
ImportantProof: Four are a single chain

The result from the previous step is used exactly as is in the proof that follows. The framework for the answer is collected in Section 14.

2 MDP Components Review

2.1 Sequential Decision Making and Uncertainty

  • Instead of performing an action once and finishing, decisions are made sequentially.
  • Since there is uncertainty in the system, instead of a method that predetermines the sequence of actions (open-loop), it is optimized in the form of a policy (state → action rule) so that the correct action can be taken even if an unexpected state is reached.
  • Immediate rewards measure only the gains of the current state or action and cannot measure long-term gains. Therefore, supervised learning cannot be applied directly, and it becomes a separate problem known as reinforcement learning.

2.2 Component

Element Notation Meaning
Status System status (location, speed, inventory, etc.)
Behavior Adjustable input (acceleration, order quantity, etc.)
Reward Immediate gain. Future gain not measured
Transition Probability Stochastic Dynamics.
  • Reward design is important. In complex problems, reward tuning is as difficult as policy learning (reward engineering). Although LLMs can assist with reward design, manual tuning may still be necessary to precisely match desired system specifications.
  • In finite intervals, transition probabilities and rewards may depend on time (non-stationary). Therefore, a subscript is attached, as in .

2.3 Decision Rules vs. Policy

  • Decision Rule — A mapping that sends a state to an action at a single point in time (snapshot)
  • Policy — A collection of decision rules from all points in time
  • Type: deterministic / stochastic(randomized), Markov / history-dependent
  • Stationary Policy: has the same policy for all
ImportantWhy distinguish decision rules and policies in finite intervals

This is because, in finite intervals, using different decision rules at each time step is actually optimal. On the other hand, in an infinite interval discounting MDP, using the same decision rule every time is optimal (stationary policy), so the two are not strictly distinguished and are simply referred to as “policies.”

2.3.1 Why is the same decision rule sufficient for infinite intervals?

This is because there is no clock. In an infinite interval, the remaining time is always infinite, so the problem in state at time and the problem in state at time 0 are identical. The same problem yields the same answer.

(when is time-invariant.) Therefore, both sides of the Bellman equation become the same function (fixed-point problem), and

Since does not appear in argmax, the same can be used at every time step. For the proof of optimality, since there is no terminal condition, uniqueness of fixed points of the contraction mapping is used instead of induction: and since the unique fixed point of is , .

Example where policy changes at different times over a finite interval (Investment vs. Consumption)

  • State 1: Consume → Reward 1, Maintain State 1 / Invest → Reward 0, Move to State 2
  • State 2: Reward 5 per step (Absorption State),
Optimal action for state 1
0 0 –
5 Consumption
10 Investment
15 Investment

Just before the deadline, consumption is optimal because there is no time to recover an investment. The remaining time creates a time dependency on the decision rule. (This time dependency does not disappear even if a discount of is applied. Since is multiplied commonly to all action candidates at time point , this factor itself does not change argmax, and the cause of the change in the decision rule is still the remaining time. Of course, since the value of changes the relative weight of future rewards, a different policy than in a problem without a discount may be optimal.)

TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)

Q1. Why is the behavioral sequence optimized in the form of a policy rather than being predetermined in a system with uncertainty?

A. Since the next state is determined probabilistically, the state → action rule must be optimized to produce an action appropriate to that state even if an unexpected state is reached.

Q2. Why cannot this be solved like supervised learning by looking only at immediate rewards?

A. This is because immediate rewards only measure the gains of the current state or behavior and fail to measure long-term gains.

Q3. Why are decision rules and policies distinguished in finite intervals?

A. This is because using different decision rules at each time point is actually optimal for finite intervals (the remaining time is different).

3 Definition of Finite-Horizon MDP

NoteDefinition

The finite interval MDP is the tuple . The newly appearing element is horizon length .

MDP Problem:

3.1 Difference from infinite interval

  • Time does not flow infinitely and stops at .
  • Reward and transition probabilities can depend on time.

3.2 Why is terminal compensation instead of ?

The action to be taken at time is not of interest. If is taken, becomes , and by repeating this, if is taken, reaches . If an action is taken at , becomes , but interest is limited to exactly . Therefore, the last term does not consider the effect of the action. This is the first characteristic of a finite horizon.

3.3 Number of entries: vs

The terms of the objective function are : stage reward (, action present) + terminal reward 1 (, action absent).

You can remember it as a fence post structure.

  • State → Point → Items
  • Action → Interval between states (transition) → items
  • Policy → decision rules
  • e.g.: If , then

3.4 Why is it difficult to solve (Difficult to solve — Why?)

The optimization target is not a number, but functions, and the number of candidates explodes combinatorially.

When , , even if only deterministic Markov policies are counted

Policy Enumeration Number of values of DP
64 12
500

Also, is coupled. Changing alters the distribution of , which changes the importance of in each state. Therefore, they cannot be optimized separately for each term.

DP breaks this combination from the back: Since serves as summary information indicating that “the rest has already been handled best,” at time step , only one action needs to be chosen. This is possible because (i) the reward is the sum of terms per time step, and (ii) due to Markov properties. (The actual computational complexity of DP, including the sum of the next state, is .)

TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)

Q1. How is this different from the infinite interval problem?

A. Time stops at , and reward/transition probabilities can depend on time.

Q2. Why is the last term instead of ?

A. The action at time point only affects , because interest extends exactly up to .

Q3. Why is this problem difficult to solve?

A. This is because the optimization targets are functions , and since they are coupled to each other through state distributions, they cannot be optimized separately.

4 Example: Stochastic Inventory Control

This is a finite-horizon MDP widely used in logistics and industrial engineering.

Element Meaning
Inventory quantity of at time
Order quantity of at time
Probabilistic demand at time , (assuming estimated from past data)

System Equation (Excess demand is lost):

Since is a random variable, it is a probabilistic system injected with randomness.

4.1 State·Behavior·Reward

  • (: Storage capacity)
  • — The set of actions depends on the state. If ordered further, there is no place to store it. Thanks to this constraint, is guaranteed.
  • — Rewards can be set in various ways and are not the core of this example.
TipReference

It is natural for actual profit to be proportional to the sales volume , and thus comes into the reward. At this point, if is calculated in advance and inserted into , the MDP form is maintained where is a function unique to .

4.2 Three cases of transition probability

Case Reason
The next stock cannot be greater than the current stock after an order (impossible)
The left term of is activated → exactly one is determined as
The right-hand side (0) of

The key point is that is a many-to-one event. If it is , the probability is taken as is because it is one-to-one, and if it is , multiple come together as one, so the sum is taken. The reason the equality sign is included in is that the stock becomes exactly 0 even when it is .

Numerical example: , , (),

Probability
0 3 0.1 ()
1 2 0.3 ()
2 1 0.4 ()
0 0.2 ()

4.3 General Principle

When encountering a stochastic dynamics system , transition probabilities can be mechanically constructed.

The inventory problem applies to the cases and , and these three cases are the result of expanding this sum. This perspective leads to the subsequent extension of continuous control.

TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)

Q1. Why is the transition probability 0 when ?

A. This is an impossible event because the next stock cannot be greater than the current stock after the order.

Q2. Why is the sum taken only when ?

A. This is because is a many-to-one event that sends all cases where demand is one . also includes an equality sign because the inventory becomes exactly 0.

Q3. Why does the behavior set depend on the state as ?

A. This is because if you order more than that, you will exceed the storage capacity and there will be no place to store it.

5 Value Function

Instead of optimizing immediately, we first deal with policy evaluation, which calculates the expected cumulative reward of the given policy .

NoteDefinition (Value Function)

is the expected cumulative reward (return) when executing policy starting from state at time .

  • return = cumulative reward.
  • Relationship with the original objective function: For the initial distribution , .
  • depends only on .

5.1 Difference from infinite interval

  1. The starting point is important. In an infinite interval, the value function had no time dependency because “the horizon is infinite, so it does not matter when it starts.” In a finite interval, even in the same state, the value differs depending on the remaining time, so is a different function at each time point.
  2. There is a terminal condition.

5.2 Q) is?

Since the start is , is an empty sum (0), and the only remaining thing is because the condition is .

ImportantTwo characteristics of a finite interval value function
  1. The value function is time-dependent. (2) It has terminal conditions and its value is equal to the terminal compensation function.

5.3 Relationship between definition (sum form) and recursion

The definition is in the form of a sum, and the recursion is an expression derived by breaking down the definition one step at a time. This structure is equivalent to an infinite interval.

Definition (Sum form) Recursion
Infinite interval (Fixed point problem)
Finite interval (backward calculation)

In the finite interval, the left side and the right side are different functions, so there is no self-referencing. Starting from , the process is completed by calculating each step once. In the infinite interval, is present on both sides, so the linear equation must be solved or converged iteratively.

TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)

Q1. What is the meaning of in words without a definition?

A. Expected value of future cumulative reward (return) when starting from state at time and following policy .

Q2. What is ? What is the reason?

A. . The sum is empty, the remainder is , and the condition is set to .

Q3. What are the two characteristics of a finite interval value function compared to an infinite interval value function?

A. (1) Depends on the starting time. (2) Has a terminal condition, and its value is equal to the terminal compensation function.

6 Optimal Policy and Optimal Value Function

6.1 Optimal Policy

It is a policy that is of greater than or equal value to any other policy, regardless of the starting state. It can be considered the solution to the previous optimization problem.

6.2 ε-optimal policy

An optimal policy does not always exist (it always exists for finite and ). When it does not exist, using an ε-optimal policy poses no practical problem.

  • Meaning: If you add ε, it beats all policies ⇔ Within ε of the optimal value. It is a policy that arbitrarily approaches the optimal performance.
  • ε must hold for all .

Example without optimal policy: , , . No matter which is chosen, there is no maximum value because there is a larger . is unattainable. If we set it to , it becomes (), so it is ε-optimal.

Situations where the optimal policy disappears: the action space is not closed, rewards and transitions are discontinuous at boundaries, and the argmax selection problem is measurable in a continuous space.

6.2.1 sup and max

  • : The largest element of the set (may not exist)
  • (supremum, least upper bound): ① an upper bound of every element, and ② for any , there exists an element greater than . If finite, it always exists.
  • Example: In , does not exist but . If exists, then .
  • ② is the basis for the existence of the ε-optimal policy. The question of the existence of the optimal policy ultimately boils down to “ is achieved”.
  • Pair: (infimum) is a generalization of . It appears in cost minimization problems.

6.3 Optimum value function

NoteDefinition (Optimal Value Function)

WarningNotation caution

The consensus start must be . If written as , (i) is broken, (ii) the past reward is not determined solely by the condition (it is an inverse conditional probability dependent on the initial distribution), and (iii) actions after time point cannot change the past, so there is no reason to include them in the optimization target.

  • The maximum value of the cumulative reward expectation that maximizes the policy at each time point.
  • is effectively the maximization of the remaining time decision rule .
  • represents the best possible performance. If the initial state is input, it is the maximum expected cumulative reward that the MDP can obtain in that state.
  • If an optimal policy exists, by definition .

6.3.1 Q) is?

No action is taken at the last point in time . Since the policy only includes up to , the last state is fixed even if is attached, so this term is not affected by any policy.

ImportantOrganize

Whether for policy evaluation or the optimal value function, the terminal condition is given by the terminal compensation function.

6.3.2 Subtle point

The definition of takes for each separately. Therefore, it is not self-evident that “a single is simultaneously optimal in all ,” and showing this is the deterministic Markov policy optimality theorem that follows.

Numerical Example (Two-State MDP, , ):

Policy
Always action 1
Optimal (including )

The difference of 0.5 is the effect of choosing action 2 in future state 2 () reflected as a probability of 0.5. is the value when the choice of the entire remaining time is optimal, not just the current action.

TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)

Q1. What is ? What is the reason?

A. . Since the policy includes only up to and there is no action at time , this term is not affected by any policy even if is attached.

Q2. What does represent?

A. The maximum expected cumulative reward that an MDP can obtain when starting from the initial state given at time 0, i.e., the best performance.

Q3. How would you define an ε-optimal policy in words?

A. If ε is added to the value of that policy, it is greater than any other policy in all states. That is, it is a policy that arbitrarily approaches optimal performance.

Q4. What is a simple example where an optimal policy does not exist?

A. , , . but there is no to achieve.

7 Finite Interval Policy Evaluation (Policy Evaluation)

7.1 Idea: Immediate reward + Expected value of the next state

The timing is important. The current reward is that of time point , and for the next state value to be accurately decomposed, the value function of time point must be used. The condition applies at time point .

  • deterministic: There is no randomness in the behavior, so it is determined as . The expected value falls only on , and the distribution is .
  • stochastic: Since the behavior is also given by a distribution, we must take the expected value by multiplying by the behavior distribution one more time in addition to the randomness of the next state. It is important not to forget this part.

7.1.1 The reason why there is no action sum in the deterministic equation

The action term has not disappeared; rather, the sum has collapsed into a single term. Since the deterministic policy is the Dirac delta , substituting it into the stochastic equation leaves only the term. What has disappeared is the average of actions , and the action is substituted as in the place of .

9 Optimality of Deterministic Markov Policy

9.1 Fundamental Question

Under what conditions is it optimal to use deterministic Markov decision rules at each time point?

Answer: Finite MDP(, finite) — more precisely, when the maximizer(argmax) on the right-hand side of the Bellman equation exists. Finiteness is a sufficient condition to guarantee the existence of argmax.

  • Why Determinism Is Sufficient: The value of the probabilistic decision rule is . Randomization offers no benefit as it is merely a convex combination of values. Equality applies only when places mass only on the argmax set. (e.g., , shuffling action 2 from state 1 with probability results in , a strictly loss.)
  • Why Markov is Enough: Once you reach , future rewards depend solely on your current state and future actions. How you got there does not affect (the past is sunk).

Cases where conditions are broken: absence of a maximizer (continuous action space), when the objective function is not a sum of expectations (risk-sensitive objective, constrained MDP), when the state is not fully observable (POMDP), when there is an adversary (mixed strategies in games).

9.2 Basic assumption: Why is it a finite MDP?

This is to show a mathematically clean result. If it is not a finite set, there is no guarantee that argmax exists, and then we have to deal with the ε-optimal policy (arbitrary precision approximation), which leads to focusing on technical details rather than the idea.

9.3 Cleanup

NoteTheorem (Optimality of Deterministic Markov Policies)

The deterministic Markov policy defined by is the optimal policy, and for all it is .

Conclusion: In finite MDPs, the optimal policy can be found by considering only deterministic Markov policies.

  • deterministic: Maps one state to one action. Markov: Uses only current state information.
  • “Optimal” means that no matter when it starts or what state it starts in, always delivers maximum performance.
  • Symbol: Used for set membership because there can be multiple (ties) maximization actions.
  • While deterministic policies are sufficient, there are cases where randomized policies are advantageous from a learning perspective (discussed in reinforcement learning).

9.3.1 What this theorem means

  1. There is a way to make it. Even if you do not optimize functions at once, an optimal policy is assembled by selecting argmax for each cell from the back.
  2. Optimal for all . The latter part of the optimal policy is also optimal for the remaining problem (the remainder of the optimal path is also optimal).
  3. A policy is a reaction rule. Even if things do not go according to plan due to uncertainty, applying again from the destination state restores it to optimality.

Why one step argmax is the overall optimal: This is because argmax contains not only but also . Since represents the “value when the subsequent steps are optimized,” the current choice is the best under the assumption that “the subsequent steps are optimized.” And since is defined in the same way at all subsequent points in time, the assumption becomes reality. (e.g., in the investment-consumption problem; looking only at the current reward in state 1, it is consumption, but since , is an investment.)

What is not said: that the optimal policy is unique (multiple if tied), that the action is the same at every time step, that argmax needs to be done at only one time step (it must be argmax at all times steps), and that the predetermined order of actions is optimal.

10 Stochastic Optimum Policy

  1. We confirmed that a deterministic optimal policy can be created. How is a stochastic optimal policy created?

Consider the case where there are multiple maximizers. Since optimal performance is maintained regardless of which one is chosen, if you assign probabilities to the optimal actions such that their sum is 1, it becomes a randomized optimal policy.

  • Example: There are three optimal actions
    • deterministic: Assign one of them (e.g., ) as the policy output
    • randomized: probabilistically selects among actions of equal performance
  • argmax It is not optimal to place mass on actions outside the set.
  • The question of when randomization and when determinism are advantageous is covered in reinforcement learning (e.g., exploration in situations where the model is unknown).

WarningThe existence of an optimal policy is not guaranteed

In continuous problems, argmax may not exist. In such cases, an ε-optimal policy is used. In fact, when solving continuous problems with reinforcement learning, errors larger than ε occur. Most, and virtually all, reinforcement learning algorithms fail to find an optimal policy, and the very purpose of reinforcement learning is to find a sufficiently good approximation policy.

13.7 New problems arising in continuous control

  1. Maximum value may not exist.
  2. Optimization is difficult because the action space is wide. Although there are algorithms for cases such as when the objective function is concave, it is generally difficult to find a maximizing action.
  3. If the state space is continuous, initialization can be done in the form of a function, but updates must hold for all real numbers.

13.8 Dioxide and the Curse of Dimensions

If the state space is , discretize. If discretized to points, the optimal value and policy are calculated only at those three points, and discretization error is introduced (perfect information is not transmitted at every step).

Generalized: 1-dimensional point → 2-dimensional point → -dimensional point. Computational load and memory increase exponentially.

ImportantCurse of Dimensionality

DP breaks down difficult problems into many easy problems, but the number of these easy problems can become too large. If continuous control is simply discretized, this exponential increase is immediately felt. The location of the difficulty has shifted from an “explosion of policy numbers ()” to an “explosion of state numbers.”

Solution Approach: Instead of discretization, define a function architecture of the value function (or policy) and learn and optimize its weights. Approximating the value function and policy with a neural network is deep reinforcement learning (deep RL).

  4. Finite , guarantee the existence of argmax and the optimal policy.

15 Final cleanup

  • Using DP, the optimal value function for each time step in a finite interval can be calculated, and if a maximizer exists, the optimal policy can also be found.
  • This is an algorithm suitable for ideal cases (small-scale problems). As the state and action space grows, it encounters computational complexity issues, so an approximation approach is ultimately required.

4 Basic matrix form I

Diagonal matrix: Non-zero elements are present only on the main diagonal.

Identity Matrix: .

Block Diagonal Matrix: Square blocks are placed on the diagonals and the rest are 0. The sizes of the blocks may differ.

5 Basic Matrix Form II

Exchange (Inversion) Matrix : Reverses row/column order.

Lower triangular matrix : Non-zero elements only on the main diagonal and below it. Upper triangular matrix : Non-zero elements only on the main diagonal and above it. The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal elements.

Vandermonde Matrix: Each column is a geometric sequence with a common ratio of .

When is positive (), it becomes , so if are distinct from each other, it is invertible. This fact serves as the basis for the statement in the DFT below that “decomposition into distinct frequencies is unique.” The DFT matrix is the Vandermonde matrix .

6 Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)

6.1 Definition

DFT sends the complex sequence with length to .

(The imaginary unit is sometimes written as or . Here, is used.)

TipOne-sentence summary

DFT is a transformation that converts a signal of length into a coordinate system based on complex sinusoidal waves, and IDFT is the process of synthesizing the original signal from those coordinates. It is invertible because it only changes the representation without discarding or adding information.

6.2 Forward DFT is an inner product that measures “how similar” they are

basis vectors

Let’s set it as . is a complex sinusoidal wave whose phase rotates by per sample. Then

, that is, is the value obtained by projecting (inner product) onto .

The multiplied reverses the phase of by a constant amount for each sample.

  • If the frequency component is present within , the phase rotation of that component is exactly canceled out, causing all terms to point in the same direction and to increase due to constructive interference.
  • Otherwise, the terms rotate around the circle and cancel out, resulting in .

is the frequency , the intensity of the component, and is the phase of that component.

6.3 Reason why the inverse transformation holds: Orthogonality

The key equation is

Proof. Let . If (both are ), then since is not a multiple of , we have and . By the geometric series formula

If , then since all terms are 1, the sum is .

That is, any two distinct bases have an inner product of 0 (orthogonal) and the inner product with itself is . Since the result depends only on the difference and not on each , the same logic applies regardless of which pair is chosen.

Now, if we substitute the forward equation into the IDFT

Thanks to orthogonality, only the term survives, and the factor accounts for the basis-vector energy . The IDFT

If read as , it is equivalent to the general rule “in an orthogonal basis expansion, coefficient = (inner product)/(norm² of the basis)”.

Check all pairs in . , , , .

pair inner product

pairs are all 0.

Small example. If (pure frequency ), then . It stands as only at the coordinate , and upon inverse transformation, it is restored to .

6.4 Geometry of Orthogonality: Polygons are Closed

When viewed in the complex plane, the inner product is the endpoint of the head-to-tail path formed by connecting points on the unit circle. If , it returns exactly to the starting point after steps, closing the polygon, and the sum of the edge vectors of the closed polygon is 0.

  • , : One step 120°, equilateral triangle closes → sum 0.
  • : Square. If , it moves back and forth 180° but also closes.
  • , : Star shape (multiple turns) but closes.
  • If is not an integer, then is opened as a polygon and the sum is not 0.

Orthogonality is determined not by a single angle value, but by “whether one step rotation angle × is an integer multiple of 360°”. Whether it is 120° or 90°, if this condition is satisfied, it is orthogonal.

6.5 Why is it decomposed into frequencies?

6.5.1 Unknowns = Equation

The object being split is not each individual element, but the entire sequence (one vector). However, from the perspective of synthesis, each element is the sum of the values contributed by frequency components at that point in time.

The sequence length has digits , i.e., degrees of freedom . To write this as the sum of sinusoidal waves

  • If the number of coefficients is less than , not all values can be met (the equation has more unknowns).
  • If the coefficients are greater than , there are infinitely many solutions, so the decomposition is not unique.

When the coefficients ZZZPH0000511ZZZ are , this equation is a square Vandermonde system, and if are different, there is exactly one solution.

6.5.2 Reason why you shouldn’t shorten: zero space

From , if and , then , so the null space exists: . Since distinct lead to the same , restoration is impossible. For example, if only is used, the directional component of disappears entirely.

6.5.3 Exactly Personal reason: Periodicity and aliasing

. On integer samples, frequencies and are indistinguishable (aliasing). There are only distinct basis vectors, and since they are all orthogonal, they form an orthogonal basis for exactly .

The DFT considers as a signal repeating with period . The sinusoidal waves that can be entered into the period signal are only harmonics that are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency , and in discrete time, it repeats times.

6.5.4 Why equal interval frequencies of all things?

As long as there are only distinct frequencies, “decomposition” is possible because the Vandermonde is invertible. The reason the DFT chooses (units at equal intervals) is due to orthogonality. With an orthogonal basis, coefficients are calculated using a single inner product without simultaneous equations, and the inverse matrix is given for free as (normalization basis).

6.5.5 If you extend it: zero-padding and frame

If we append zeros to to make the length and perform -point DFT

, that is, the DTFT has been sampled more densely. Since the DTFT is already determined by values, this is interpolation. The spectrum appears smoother and peak positions become easier to read, but the resolution for distinguishing two nearby frequencies does not improve, as it is determined by the window length .

In this case, the vector is a frame of . If is not an integer (based on the grid)

Since it is (Dirichlet kernel), orthogonality is broken. The fact that it becomes zero only on the lattice is the fundamental reason why the DFT lattice is .

6.5.6 Cases where it can be shortened: Prior knowledge

If you know that has only frequencies, that is sufficient (low-pass filtering of band-limited signals, compression, compressed sensing of sparse spectrum). Information can be discarded only when the signal model guarantees that that part is empty.

case property
(General ) Zero space exists, cannot be restored
, integer orthogonal basis, unique·invertible
(zero-padding) overcomplete frame, overlap, spectral interpolation
+ Sparse/Band-limited assumption Restorable thanks to model

6.6 Common Misconception: “ arrows on a circle are not orthogonal”

If you divide a circle into 6 equal parts, 6 arrows emanating from the origin are created at 60° intervals, and they are clearly not orthogonal. However, in that figure, the points on the circle are not different basis vectors, but components of a single basis vector.

Meaning of the dot on the circle
Invalid drawing One by one basis vectors (arrows in a 2D plane)
Actual DFT Basis one component
  • In a 2D plane, there are at most 2 mutually orthogonal vectors. If you cram in 6, orthogonality appears impossible.
  • The DFT basis is a vector in , that is, a -dimensional space. If , it is 6-dimensional and can contain up to 6 mutually orthogonal vectors.
  • Orthogonality means that the product of two vectors with components at the same position is 0, and this is orthogonal in dimensional space.

From the smallest ZZZPH0000539ZZZ , , and are real numbers and are actually perpendicular on the plane. From onwards, the components are complex numbers and the dimension is large, so they cannot be drawn with arrows, but the same calculation holds.

Method Visible Limits

Although the geometric figure of a “right angle” must be abandoned due to its dimension, the algebraic fact that the “inner product is zero” is sufficiently visualized through waveforms and polygons.

6.7 Orthogonality Seen Through Waveforms

Plotting the components of the basis on the axis results in a sampled cos/sin waveform. Since the dot product is “multiplying and adding the same ,” it is the sum of the heights of the bars formed by multiplying the two waveforms.

  • : The product is a pure sinusoidal wave with frequency , and since it fills the exact integer period over samples, equal amounts of positive and negative values are generated, so the sum is 0. The inner product is 0 only when both the real and imaginary parts are 0.
  • : Since all products are , stacking them up gives a sum of . (The real cosine bases are of the form , so .)

6.8 Orthogonal Version

  • Orthogonal: The inner product of different bases is 0.
  • Orthonormal: Orthogonal + length of each basis is 1.

The standard basis is , so it is orthogonal but not orthonormal. If we set it to , it becomes , and the transformation is in both directions.

The standard version is (forward 1, reverse ), and the orthonormal version is (, ). The product of the two scales is the same, . Where it is placed is a matter of convention.

Differences in the orthonormal version:

  1. Symmetric Inverse Transformation. Since the basis length is 1, the division of “inner product ÷ norm²” is not necessary, and the inverse matrix is .
  2. Parseval (Energy Conservation). . The standard version is , so .
  3. Geometrically pure rotation. A unitary transformation rotates only the coordinate axes without changing lengths or angles. The standard DFT is the rotation multiplied by a scale.

e.g., , , then standard Z, , orthonormal Z, .

Meaning in Wireless Communication. If is iid noise with a variance of , the standard DFT is , and the orthonormal DFT is . The orthonormal version is more convenient when consistently comparing power/SNR in the time and frequency domains, as in OFDM.

6.9 Index convention ( vs )

Convention Scope Common uses

1-based MATLAB, Julia

The exponent of the DFT is an expression written as a number counted from 0 (the first sample is phase 0). If 1-based numbers are used, must be entered into the exponent.

MATLAB fft is the definition of this form. If you write as is to the 1-based without changing the exponents (, )

is formed, adding an unnecessary phase factor, and since the time factor is multiplied by a sinusoidal wave of frequency 1, the spectrum is shifted by one step. Example: If , the correct DFT is (flat), but without correction, it becomes (phase slope of time delay).

Fundamental reason: Since is the period for all , it covers different values once in any range of consecutive integers (the fftshift convention of setting it to is also possible). However, since which sample is defined as time 0 affects the phase, the exponents must be aligned together to maintain the reference point (“consistent phases”).

6.10 CTFT → Fourier Series → DTFT → DFT

The four transformations lead to the following two duality rules.

In one area In the opposite area
Repeat with period Discrete line with interval
Sampling at interval Repeating at period

Intuition: If a time signal is repeated with a period , the only sinusoidal waves that can fit within it are those with frequencies that are integer multiples of → The spectrum is discrete. If time is sampled with a period , frequencies and are indistinguishable on the sample (aliasing) → The spectrum is periodic.

  1. CTFT: Time continuous/aperiodic ↔︎ Frequency continuous/aperiodic.
  2. Fourier Series: Time period repetition ↔︎ Frequency discrete line.
  3. DTFT: Time sampling (Dirac comb) ↔︎ Frequency periodic (notation ).
  4. DFT: Apply both → Time discrete-period ↔︎ Frequency discrete-period. DFT samples one period of DTFT, and IDFT reconstructs one period in the time domain. FFT is an algorithm that calculates this efficiently.

To summarize, “periodic ↔︎ discrete” and “non-periodic ↔︎ continuous” form pairs.

The reason why appears in step 4 is clearly revealed.

The number of samples in one period on the time side and the number of lines in one period on the frequency side are the same . A structure in which the inputs and the outputs correspond is derived from this.

6.11.1 Matrix Definition

Each row of is a sampled complex sinusoidal wave, and the IDFT uses . Since the columns (rows) are orthonormal, (unitary).

Since , the dotted line is the solid line shifted forward by 90° (1/4 period). The complex exponent is a point on the unit circle, and projecting it onto the real axis gives cos, and projecting it onto the imaginary axis gives sin; since the two axes are perpendicular, the two projected waveforms are always offset by 90°.

The matrix is a linear transformation that converts a vector into another vector. Most vectors change direction, but vectors with special directions maintain their direction and become times their length.

The assumption that “eigenvalues are distinct” merely simplifies the proof, and by the spectrum theorem, a Hermitian matrix can always be unitarily diagonalized even with duplicate eigenvalues (one simply needs to choose an orthonormal basis within the duplicate eigenspace).

12 Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

12.1 Definition

For any

is a matrix formed by placing on the opposite diagonal and filling the rest with zeros. Unlike eigenvalue decomposition, it always exists even if it is not square and cannot be diagonalized.

Geometric meaning: All linear transformations are decomposed into rotation () → axial scale () → rotation ().

12.2 Thin SVD and Rank

If you divide into

, which is multiplied by the singular value of 0, does not contribute to so it can be discarded. The rank is the number of non-zero singular values.

Relationship between singular values and eigenvalues:

12.3 Tall matrix ()

rank . Thin SVD is , , . The columns of are the orthonormal basis of range , and the columns of generate the row space.

12.4 Wide matrix ()

rank . Thin SVD likewise , . The columns of are orthonormal right singular vectors, and generates a column space.

Yes basic subspace cleanup:

subspace basis
Column space
Left zero space
Row space
Null space

(Since , creates the null space.)

12.5 Pseudo-inverse and least squares

Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse is

(Although it is sometimes written as in some literature, it is written as here to avoid confusion with conjugate transposition.)

The year of is

Derivation. Since is unitary, length is preserved

If we set , then , so it is minimized when (), and () is independent of the objective function. Among them, if we choose () such that is minimized, then . That is, is the least squares solution with the minimum norm. If is column-complete rank, it is equal to (solution to the normal equation).

Conditional number. When fully ranked

Small singular values are greatly amplified from to , so the noise of significantly disrupts the solution (ill-conditioning). In MIMO, this phenomenon is that if the condition number of channel is large, the noise amplification of ZF detection increases.

12.6 Connection with proprietary analysis

Eigendecomposition of Gram matrices:

Derivation: and is opposite ( and 0). Therefore

  • Right singular vector = eigenvector of , left singular vector = eigenvector of .
  • The non-zero eigenvalues of the two Gram matrices are all the same, **.

Since the Gram matrix is a Hermitian PSD, the unitary diagonalization from the previous section applies, and this is the starting point for the proof of the existence of SVD.

13 Numerical verification

Code 
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def crandn(*s): return rng.standard_normal(s) + 1j*rng.standard_normal(s)
err = lambda X, Y: np.max(np.abs(X - Y))

# 1) 정규직교 DFT 행렬은 유니터리이지만 W^T W != I
N = 8
n = np.arange(N); W = np.exp(-2j*np.pi*np.outer(n, n)/N)/np.sqrt(N)
print("W^H W = I            :", err(W.conj().T @ W, np.eye(N)))
print("W x == fft(x)/sqrt(N):", err(W @ (x := crandn(N)), np.fft.fft(x)/np.sqrt(N)))
print("W^T W - I (non-zero) :", err(W.T @ W, np.eye(N)))

# 2) Circulant 대각화와 원형 컨볼루션 정리
c = crandn(N)
C = np.array([[c[(i-j) % N] for j in range(N)] for i in range(N)])
lam = np.array([np.sum(c*np.exp(2j*np.pi*k*n/N)) for k in range(N)])   # sum c_m w^{-km}
print("C = W diag(lam) W^H  :", err(C, W @ np.diag(lam) @ W.conj().T))
print("lam == DFT(first row):", err(lam, np.fft.fft(C[0])))
print("C = W^H diag(fft c) W:", err(C, W.conj().T @ np.diag(np.fft.fft(c)) @ W))

# 3) Woodbury
n_, k_ = 6, 2
A = crandn(n_, n_) + 5*np.eye(n_); B = crandn(n_, k_); Cm = crandn(k_, k_) + 3*np.eye(k_); D = crandn(k_, n_)
Ai = np.linalg.inv(A)
wood = Ai - Ai @ B @ np.linalg.inv(np.linalg.inv(Cm) + D @ Ai @ B) @ D @ Ai
print("Woodbury             :", err(wood, np.linalg.inv(A + B @ Cm @ D)))

# 4) Kronecker 성질
A2, B2 = crandn(3, 3), crandn(2, 2)
K = np.kron(A2, B2)
print("tr(A⊗B)=trA trB      :", abs(np.trace(K) - np.trace(A2)*np.trace(B2)))
print("det(A⊗B)=detA^2 detB^3:", abs(np.linalg.det(K) - np.linalg.det(A2)**2*np.linalg.det(B2)**3))
X = crandn(3, 2); Bv = crandn(2, 4)
vec = lambda M: M.reshape(-1, order="F")
print("vec(AXB)=(B^T⊗A)vecX :", err(vec(A2 @ X @ Bv), np.kron(Bv.T, A2) @ vec(X)))

# 5) SVD 의사역행렬과 최소제곱
Am = crandn(7, 4); b = crandn(7)
U, s, Vh = np.linalg.svd(Am, full_matrices=False)
Ap = Vh.conj().T @ np.diag(1/s) @ U.conj().T
print("A+ == pinv(A)        :", err(Ap, np.linalg.pinv(Am)))
print("LS solution          :", err(Ap @ b, np.linalg.lstsq(Am, b, rcond=None)[0]))
print("sigma^2 = eig(A^H A) :", err(np.sort(s**2), np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(Am.conj().T @ Am))))

item.title: Markov Decision Process
item.description:
1 Model and Policy: Fix before proof

1.1 Common Assumptions and Notation

The theorem in this article assumes a finite set of states , a non-empty finite set of actions , complete state observations, and expected cumulative reward maximization. All action sums and maximums are taken for . Rewards are real and bounded.

Symbol Meaning
State of time and selected action
Distribution of the next state; non-negative and
Rewards for this period or their conditional average
History to date
Probability of action selection in general policy
Initial state distribution
Policy-induced path distribution and its expected value
Transition matrix and reward vector averaged by normal Markov policy
Maximum absolute value norm; is a component inequality

The Markov nature of the model is the following condition.

In other words, if you know the current state and behavior, older records are not needed to predict the next state. Whether policies use the past is a separate issue.

If the reward also depends on the next state, then based on the expected total reward

can be written by averaging it as |||. is the reward for this period, and , which appears later, is the total reward from the next point in time.

1.2 Distinction between decision rules and policies

Decision rules are guidelines to use at a given point in time, and a policy is a sequence of those rules. Deterministic rules specify a single action, while probabilistic rules specify the distribution of actions.

Class Input Output
MD Current Status
MR Current Status
HD History
HR History

Deterministic choice is a probabilistic choice in which an action is assigned a probability of 1. Therefore, MD is included in MR and HD respectively, and MR and HD are included in HR. There is no general inclusion relationship between MR and HD.

A stationary Markov policy uses the same rule at every point in time. A stationary deterministic policy can also choose a different action if the state changes.

WarningMarkov policy and normal policy are different

uses only the current state, so it is a Markov policy, but it can vary depending on the time point. In a finite horizon, even for the same state, the optimal action can differ depending on the remaining time. Stationarity does not automatically follow.

The pre-fixed sequence of actions is a special policy that does not react to observed states. Therefore, in settings using a common set of actions, the value of policy optimization is not smaller than the value of fixed sequence of actions optimization. Choosing only the current highest reward is also generally not optimal, because actions change the distribution of the next state.

The reason for optimizing the policy. The reward is the immediate gain of the current choice, not the correct label itself, which is the optimal action. Therefore, it cannot be directly transformed into a supervised learning problem that maximizes only the immediate reward. Once a policy is derived, the action to be taken in a given state is specified, even if a state different from the expectation occurs.

The difficulty of policy optimization lies in the fact that the actions determined for each state influence each other through future transitions. Even in finite models with a common set of actions, there are policies that are not ZZZ deterministic. Dynamic programming (DP) solves this problem using value functions. It does not generalize to mean that “policies are functions and therefore cannot be differentiated under any circumstances.”

2 The stochastic process created by the policy

2.1 Path probability and Markovity

The probability of the finite path is the chain rule

This formula is the probability of a finite path. We apply this formula to each finite-length path event even over an infinite horizon. We do not inadvertently equate the infinite product with the probability of an individual infinite path.

Proposition. If a Markov policy is used, the sequence of states is a Markov process.

Proof. If you sum the actions

The right-hand side depends only on , not the entire past. Since the equation remains the same even if only the past of the state is given as a condition, the state column is Markov. If both the model and the policy are time-invariant, the transition matrix is also time-independent.

Intuition: If the environment moves based only on the current state and behavior, and policies also act based only on the current state, the past cannot provide additional information for the future.

WarningWhen the denominator of the conditional probability is 0

When calculating conditional probability as a ratio of probabilities, the probability of the conditional event must be positive. If the entire conditional distribution is set to zero because the denominator is zero, it does not become a probability distribution. To define the value of an unvisited state, define it as a new problem starting from that state. It is not necessary to visit that state in the original initial distribution.

Since history-dependent policies can alter the distribution of behavior based on the past, the Markovity of the state sequence cannot be concluded solely from the Markovity of the model. However, this does not mean that all history policies necessarily produce non-Markov state sequences.

3 One-period MDP: The starting point of all proofs

Perform one action at time 0 and receive a terminal reward at time 1. Let’s define.

3.1 Summary: Deterministic choice is sufficient

The optimal value in state is , and selecting the one action that gives the maximum value is optimal.

Proof. For a random action distribution

In a finite and non-empty , there exists an action that achieves a maximum value. If that action is given a probability of 1, the upper bound is achieved.

Equality condition: All actions that are must yield the maximum value. Randomizing among the best actions is harmless, but it does not produce a better value either.

Proof Structure: First, find the upper bound for an arbitrary policy, and then construct a policy that achieves that upper bound. Subsequently, the proof of finite-infinite horizon optimality also follows this structure.

Adding the constant to the total terminal reward increases all by . This is because the sum of the transition probabilities is 1. Therefore, the optimal action does not change. What is important for comparing actions is the difference in value between terminal states.

4 Finite Horizon MDP: Inverse Induction

4.1 Objective function and boundary conditions

The decision point is , and at , no action is taken and only the terminal reward is received. This section deals with finite horizons without discounting.

The remaining value of the Markov policy is

Here, means that the state at time point is set to , and the policy is applied thereafter. Policy evaluation is also calculated using a one-step decomposition.

4.2 Summary: Bellman Recursion and Optimal Policy

Define the candidate value from the back as follows.

Then is optimal even when compared to all HR policies. Each is the optimal remaining value possible at that point in time and state.

4.2.1 Proof: Inductively derives the upper bound and attainment together

1. Basic Phase . Since there are no more actions, the remaining reward for any policy is .

2. Induction to the Upper Bound. Fix an arbitrary HR policy and use as the expected remaining reward after history . From

Let’s assume . Using iterative expectation and the Markov nature of the model

The first inequality is the assumption of induction and non-negative probability, and the second inequality is mean ≤ maximum. In a history where the reach probability is 0, the same recursion can be used by defining with a specified follow-up policy and transition instead of the ratio of conditional probabilities.

3. Induction on Achieving the Upper Limit. Let us assume that if is used after time , is achieved. If is chosen at time ,

Therefore, the same policy achieves the upper bound for all points in time and states.

TipThe core of the proof

“Starting from the terminal condition, we constrain the residual value of any history-dependent policy to above. Since the state-specific argmax rule inductively achieves its upper bound, a deterministic Markov policy is sufficient.”

Intuition: Solve the last problem and use the answer as the terminal value from the immediately previous time step. Even if the past is different, if the current state and remaining time are the same, the optimal strategy to be used going forward can be shared.

4.3 Verification using two-state example

Let’s apply finite horizon and end compensation 0 to the following two state models.

Even within the same , the optimal action changes depending on the number of remaining decisions. However, this does not mean that a finite horizon optimal policy is always abnormal. There are special problems where a normal policy is also optimal.

5 Discount Infinite Horizons: Policy Evaluation

From now on, the model is time-invariant and . The policy evaluation formula is a normal Markov policy.

5.1 Definition of Return and Value

Therefore, the return converges absolutely and is integrable. The exchange of the expectation value and the infinite sum can also be justified by this upper bound. In the time-invariant model and stationary policy, since the future distribution observed from the same state is independent of the starting time, the subscript is not needed.

5.2 Monte Carlo Policy Evaluation

Fix the policy and create multiple trajectories from the same starting state, then calculate the average of each cumulative reward.

If you can observe an independent full return starting from the same state

Linearity of the expected value is used for unbiasedness, and sample independence is used for the variance formula. If the infinite horizon is cut at the step and replaced with , the sample mean is unbiased at , but is generally biased at .

Averaging many trajectories and observing each trajectory for a long time reduce other errors. There is no theorem that MC variance is always large. However, large variance can occur due to the randomness of long trajectories.

5.3 Summary: Bellman Policy Evaluation Equation

Proof Flow.

  1. Decomposes the return into .
  2. Apply iterative expectation to .
  3. Using a Markov model and Markov policy, remove previous states and actions from future conditions.
  4. Due to the time invariance of the model and policy, the remaining value at the next time step is written as .

If you connect this as an expression

If you use in the compensation term, it is the desired expression.

Note: The past is not erased solely by iteration expectation. To remove the past, Markovity of the model and policy is required, and to erase time indices, stationarity is also required.

5.4 Matrix Representation and the Existence of Inverse Matrices

Then it is . Since is a non-negative matrix where the sum of each row is 1, it is . Therefore, the matrix series converges and

The inverse matrix expression is not a simple formal transposition. Multiplying the partial sum of the series by results in , and since the last term goes to 0, it is confirmed to be the inverse matrix.

Example Verification: If is applied to the previous two state models, it is in all policies. If is always used with

If you always use , it is .

6 Bellman Operator and Proof Tool

For any value candidate

takes the average as the policy, and takes the maximum among the actions. The former is generally an affine mapping, and is not called a linear mapping because of the reward term.

6.1 Monotonicity · Constant Shift · Greed Policy

Properties Formula Reason
Monotonicity Non-negative probability; max preserves order
Constant shift Sum of transition probabilities 1
Upper bound of mean Mean ≤ Maximum
Greedy Policy Directly select maximum action

Monotonicity and constant shift hold for as well. The last equation holds for used to select the policy, but is not guaranteed for any other .

6.2 Summary: The two operators are -contraction

Policy evaluation operator. If you cancel out the reward term and limit the weighted average of the probabilities

Optimal operator. First, for two finite sequences

Verify that . If we select , it becomes , and by swapping , we also obtain the opposite direction. Therefore

Taking the maximum value for the state yields contractility.

6.3 Banach Fixed Point Theorem: Necessary Parts and Proof

In a complete metric space, if is a contraction with coefficient , then a unique fixed point exists, and converges from any starting point to that fixed point.

Existence: Since , when

It is due to completeness, and due to the continuity of contraction events.

Uniqueness: If there are two fixed points , then , so the two are equal.

Error: If contractility is repeated .

Here, since is complete, it can be applied. Therefore, and each have a unique fixed point. By the policy evaluation formula, the fixed point of the former is . The fact that the latter fixed point is the optimal value still needs to be proven.

7 Bellman Optimality and Optimal Policy

Intuition: The optimal value is the best performance achievable in the current state. The Bellman formula compares the “current reward + the discounted optimal value of the next state.” Optimization for the entire policy is represented by the maximization of the current action, but the computational burden of having to perform this maximization in all states remains.

7.1 Summary: The fixed point is the optimal value

For all HR policies, the value starting from the state at time point 0 is defined as , and

Let . Then is the only fixed point of , and a single deterministic steady-state Markov policy achieves this in all states. Therefore, the above can be written as .

7.1.1 Proof Step 1: Achievable Candidate Configurations

Let be the fixed point obtained through contractility. In each state

If you select , it becomes . Since the fixed point of the policy evaluation operator is unique,

In other words, the candidate can be achieved through actual policies.

7.1.2 Proof Step 2: Upper bound for an arbitrary policy

Since , for all

Averaging behaviors with an arbitrary HR policy and applying iterative expectations

Multiplying both sides by and taking the expected value, then adding it for , the intermediate value terms are canceled out.

In finite state space, is bounded, so . Since the complementary series can also pass the limit through the bounded supreme bound, it is .

7.1.3 Proof Step 3: Conclusion

For all policies, it is , and achieves . Therefore, it is and

The same is optimal in all states.

WarningOrder to avoid circular reasoning

When proving that “the optimal value is a Bellman fixed point,” do not write it as if it were already a definition. Write it in the order of existence of a candidate due to contractility → Greedy policy achieves the candidate → Upper bound of all policies → Candidate is the optimal value. Do not conclude the optimality of all HR policies based on a proof that compares only normal policies.

7.2 Exact conditions of stochastic optimal policy

Let , . The necessary and sufficient condition for the normal Markov policy to be optimal in all states is

Sufficientity: Since we average only the maximum actions . Due to fixed-point uniqueness .

Necessity: If , then . Therefore, in each state

Since all terms are non-negative, the difference between actions with positive probabilities must be 0.

Deterministic policies are also included in the probabilistic policy class. The absence of ties does not mean that there are no optimal policies within the probabilistic policy class, but rather that non-degenerate randomization is impossible. Furthermore, the above condition applies to optimality in all states. When maximizing only of a specific initial distribution, the selection of unreached states does not need to be optimal.

7.3 Fixed point repetition

That is, the fixed-point iteration converges to the optimal value. In policy evaluation, is iterated over instead of .

8 Commonly Mistaken Assumptions

Sentences that are easy to misuse Accurate expressions
Since it is an MDP, the state column is always Markov It is guaranteed under a Markov policy. It can be broken under an HR policy.
Calculate as a single finite horizon Generally, since remaining time is needed, use .
Acts even at the last point in time By convention of this document, the last action is , .
Proof of contractility on a finite horizon is required A terminal condition and a finite number of backward inductions are sufficient.
If it is an infinite horizon, time indices can be erased Time invariance of models and policies is also necessary.
The same fixed point proof applies to
If it terminates almost certainly, the expected total reward is always finite Separate conditions such as the integrability of the termination time are required.
argmax always exists Here, it exists because the action set is not empty and is finite.
The existence of an optimal fixed point is proof of optimality It must be achieved by the policy and shown to be the upper bound of all comparison policies.
Stochastic policies are always worse than deterministic policies Mixing only optimal actions yields the same value.
The optimal value across all initial distributions is the same as the optimal value in one If you look only at a specific distribution, you might miss the difference in unvisited states.
A sufficiently long truncated MC is exactly uncomfortable Truncation bias can be reduced but is generally not zero.

9 Proof problems to solve on your own

Let’s verify the logic of each proof directly through the problems below. It is helpful to organize the steps in the order of Assumption → Claim → Tools Used → Upper Limit → Achievement or Limit. Hints can be viewed after attempting the solution.

9.1 Problem 1. One-period randomization and equality condition

Finiteness was used to guarantee the existence of the maximum value and argmax. Although the inequality that the mean cannot exceed the upper bound holds even in situations more general than finiteness, the existence of the optimal action must be verified separately.

9.2 Problem 2. MD policy is better than HR policy in a finite horizon

9.4 Problem 4. Bellman Policy Evaluation Formula

Derive the Bellman evaluation formula for a stationary Markov policy from the return definition of . Indicate separately where iterative expectation, Markovity, and stationarity are used. Also, explain why is invertible.

9.7 Problem 7. Stochastic Optimum Policy

TipHint

9.8 Problem 8. Constant Movement and Finite Horizon

item.title: Distance between Vector Space and Probability Densities
item.description:
1 Overview

This document consists of two parts.

  1. Vector Space and Inner Product Space. Establishes a framework that views signals as vectors and assigns length, angle, orthogonality, and distance.
  2. Distance between probability densities. Since the set of probability densities is not a vector space, norm-based distances are not natural. As alternative tools, we deal with mixture models, manifold perspectives, Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, and Chernoff distances, and finally, we prove the relationship that the Chernoff distance is equal to the KL value at a specific point.

In the whole, represents the natural logarithm (). Even if the base is changed, all conclusions remain valid as long as they are unified to the same base (Section 5.5.3.1).

2 Linear vector space

2.1 Definition and Vector Addition Axioms

The linear vector space is a structure in which two operations, vector addition and scalar multiplication, are given to a collection of elements (vectors) and satisfy the following axioms. Vectors are written as , and scalars are written as (usually or ), an element of the field .

Vector Addition Axiom

  1. Closure:

  5. Additive inverse: For every angle , there exists such that

2.2 Scalar and Field

To write the axioms of scalar product, “what a scalar is” must first be determined. A scalar forms a field . For addition and multiplication, the field

  • Associative law, Commutative law, Distributive law
  • Additive identity , Multiplicative identity
  • Additive inverse of all elements, multiplicative inverse of all elements other than

It is a structure that has . The last condition distinguishes the field from a ring and enables division.

The scalar product is a mapping

. The fact that the result belongs back to is the closure of the scalar product.

NoteThe reason a sieve is needed

In the proof of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality , the optimal coefficient is used, which is an operation of dividing by the scalar . Furthermore, by abstracting , and can be handled at once, allowing complex baseband signals to also fit into the same framework.

2.3 Scalar product axiom

  4. Distributive law: ,

Since it is a component-wise operation, the properties of the field are applied to each component as they are, and all axioms hold.

2.5 Example:

is a set of finite energy signals. Operations are defined point by point.

From this perspective, each function is a vector, and it can be viewed as a “vector with a continuous number of components” where time acts as an index of the components. This is an infinite dimension example corresponding to the finite dimension .

The statement “all vector space axioms are satisfied” means that if the axioms are verified one by one, they all pass. Verification is divided into two categories.

(1) Axioms inherited from point-by-point operations. Since the operation at each time point is an operation between scalars , the properties of the field are transferred as they are. For example, the commutative law is

(2) Axiom to be verified in practice: Closure. Sums or scalar multiplications must not extend to infinity of energy.

While no distinction is necessary when looking only at the vector space axioms, it is necessary for the positive definiteness of the inner product . This is because a function that is not zero only on a set of measure zero is different from the zero function.

3.1 Axiom of the inner product (1–3)

In real vector space, the inner product is a mapping that maps scalars to two vectors to create the concepts of length, angle, and orthogonality.

Writing only “first slot” is not because it does not hold in the second slot, but because it is derived from symmetry, so there is no need to write it as an axiom.

Therefore, the real inner product is a bilinear form that is linear in both digits. Since symmetry implies that linearity in one digit is sufficient for the other to follow, this follows the convention of writing the minimum number of axioms.

3.1.2 When this distinction actually becomes important

(a) Complex number field. If the symmetry changes to the conjugate symmetry

4.4 Manifold perspective

The idea is not to force density into a linear space, but to view the set of allowable densities as a manifold. A manifold is locally flat, allowing for the definition of tangents and geodesics, but it can be curved overall. On this, distance is measured not by a linear norm, but by geodesic distance or information-geometric distance (Fisher–Rao, etc.).

4.4.1 Intuition: The ruler’s markings must be different at each position

The distance in linear space depends only on the difference . The scale is the same everywhere. However, it is natural to measure the “degree of difference” between distributions by how easy it is to distinguish, and this varies depending on location.

Example 1: Same parameter difference, different difficulty of distinction. In

  • vs : They are virtually the same distribution.

are approximately and , respectively. The scale is dense at the smallest point of .

Example 2: Longitude on a map. The actual distance of 1° of longitude is approximately 111 km at the equator and approximately 55 km at 60° latitude. Since the actual distance varies depending on the location even with the same coordinate difference, a metric is required to correct the scale for each location. This analogy is accurate only in the sense that “the scale changes depending on the location,” and the actual geometry of the Gaussian family is hyperbolic geometry.

Example 3: Path connecting two distributions. The midpoint from to is created using two methods, as shown in the figure below. Mixing density values results in a bimodal distribution, while mixing log density shifts one peak.

4.4.2 Terminology

Term Meaning
Manifold A space in which the neighborhood of every point corresponds smoothly to the open set . The correspondence is called a chart (coordinate system).
Tangent space The set of velocity vectors of curves at a single point. It is a local planar approximation and is a vector space.
Riemannian metric The inner product assigned to the tangent space of each point . may vary from point to point.
Geodesic The curve connecting two points with the locally minimum length (a “straight line” on a surface).

The length and geodetic distance of curve is

4.4.3 Examples of manifolds

  • Circle : A one-dimensional manifold in a two-dimensional plane. Small arcs look like straight pieces.
  • Circle, parabola, hyperbola, cubic curve: All are one-dimensional manifolds that can be closed, open, or extend infinitely.
  • Sphere, torus, double torus, Klein bottle etc.: 2-dimensional manifolds. Distances within a surface are measured by geodesics that follow the curvature. On a sphere, great circles are geodesics, which is the reason why flight paths between continents appear curved.

4.4.4 Reasons to view density as a manifold
