item.title: Stochastic Processes - I
item.description:
1 Overall flow

The framework of the logic covered in this document is summarized in the following single line.

And finally, we cover two representative stochastic processes — Wiener processes (non-normal processes) and Gaussian processes (processes where everything is determined solely by the mean and covariance).

Steps Key Questions Key Tools
Basic Definitions What is a Stochastic Process? Sample Function, Time-dependent Random Variable
Stationarity Does the statistical property depend on the time origin? SSS, WSS
Autocorrelation How similar are the two time points?
PSD How is power distributed by frequency? Wiener–Khinchin Theorem
LTI Filtering How Does a Filter Change the Spectrum of a Stochastic Process?
Wiener Process What happens when white noise is accumulated?
Gaussian Process When Is the Second Statistic Sufficient? Multivariate Gaussian

2 Basic Definition of a Stochastic Process

2.1 A stochastic process as a function of two variables

Random / Stochastic Process is a rule that assigns a single time function to each outcome in the sample space.

In other words, the stochastic process is a function of two variables, and , and depending on which variable is fixed, it becomes a completely different object.

Fixing Obtained Name
Fixed, Varying Deterministic time function Sample function / realization
Fixed, Changing Random variable , Distribution Random variable at time
Both fixed One real number Sample value
Both change Collection of sample functions Ensemble
ImportantThe sample function must be defined over the entire domain

Each sampling function must be defined across the entire time domain of interest. Constructions such as “for some , there is a value only at some time points” are not allowed.

2.2 Reading horizontally vs. reading vertically

The figure below shows the dual interpretation of a stochastic process at once.

  • Read Horizontally: Each curve is a sampling function corresponding to a different result . The waveform observed today and the waveform observed tomorrow may be different curves.
  • Reading Vertically: If a vertical line is drawn at a specific time , the set of points where the curves intersect that line becomes the samples of the random variable , and the distribution is .

3 Stationarity

3.1 The precise meaning of joint distribution

Since the definition of stationarity involves the joint distribution, let us first clarify this concept. When two random variables are defined on the same sample space, the joint CDF is

, and the joint PDF is (if it exists) . The degree joint distribution of a stochastic process is an extension of this.

WarningNot the intersection of random variables

The object to which the intersection is taken is not the random variable itself, but the event . And “distribution” refers to viewing the probability of that intersection event as a function of . To summarize:

Joint Distribution = “Probability that events generated from each occur simultaneously” expressed as a function of

3.2 Strict-Sense Stationarity (SSS)

NoteDefinition (SSS)

The fact that the stochastic process is strong stationary (SSS) means that the joint amplitude distribution is invariant under common time shifts.

This equation must hold for all three of the following:

  1. Random Order (No matter how many times you select)
  2. Random set of times
  3. Random movement

Intuitively, this means that the process appears statistically the same regardless of when the observation begins (where the clock’s origin is set).

TipQ. Does the SSS condition need to hold only in a specific , or must it hold in all ?

must hold for all . That is exactly what the definition of means.

If the joint distribution is invariant for only one specific (and its integer multiples), this is not “independent of the time origin” but a much weaker property that “statistics repeat with a period ,” and such a process is separately called a cyclostationary process. (e.g., a digital communication signal modulated with a symbol period )

Additionally, the condition is simultaneously applied with the order and the “randomness” of the time set. If either of these is restricted to a “specific case,” it is no longer SSS but becomes weakened stationarity. A typical example of weakening is the WSS shown below.

3.2.1 Things that follow from SSS

(1) : Linear distribution independent of time → Mean and variance are constant

Applying the SSS definition to results in , meaning the marginal distribution is the same for all times. Therefore

In a general stochastic process, the mean is also a function of , but in SSS, since the PDF itself is fixed, the mean is also fixed.

WarningThe converse does not hold

“Fixed PDF ⇒ Fixed Mean” is true, but “Fixed Mean ⇒ Fixed PDF” is false. For example, consider a process that follows a uniform distribution at some time and a Gaussian distribution at others, but has a mean that is always 0. Since the mean is fixed but the distribution varies from time to time, it is not SSS. This distinction serves as the motivation for introducing the concept of WSS separately.

(2) : Autocorrelation depends only on the time difference — Proven in the Autocorrelation Function section below.

3.3 Autocorrelation Function

NoteDefinition

In random variable theory, the expected value of the product of two random variables is called correlation. Here, we choose two times , but since they are ultimately two random variables derived from the same stochastic process, it is called autocorrelation, meaning “correlation with itself.” It measures how “moves together” (is similar) the amplitudes of the two times.

3.3.1 Why does the steady process depend only on the time difference ?

The key point is that the expected value is completely determined by the joint distribution alone. The right-hand side of the above definition depends only on .

SSS definition() is for all

It requires . Since it holds for all , you may substitute a specific value .

Since the two joint distributions are the same, the expected value calculated from them is also the same.

The right-hand side does not individually include , but only the difference . Therefore

Intuitively, if the time origin does not affect the statistics, the only information remaining between two time points is “how far apart”. Since and are both , they must have the same correlation in a stationary process. This can also be written as follows.

TipWhat was actually used in this derivation is not the entire SSS

In the derivation above, only the time-shift invariance of the joint distribution was used. That is, to obtain “ depends only on ,” it is not necessary to go up to SSS (all orders), and second-order invariance is sufficient. This observation is the design principle of WSS.

3.3.2 The meaning of and “Univariate vs. Multivariate”

TipQ. Is a time shift, and does it mean ? Should I understand this as multivariate rather than univariate?

The beginning part is correct. If you substitute

It is . (If defined as , it becomes , but as shown below, in the real number WSS process is an even function, so it is the same regardless of how it is defined.)

The expression “multivariate” is accurate only when distinguishing between two perspectives.

Perspective Answer
Number of input variables for function Normal process: is a 2-variable function. Normal process: is reduced to a single 1-variable function
Probability structure required to calculate that value The joint (bivariate) distribution of the two random variables is required → In this sense, “multivariate” is correct

cannot be calculated from the marginal distributions of each time point alone (except for the special case where the two time points are independent). That is, “ is a single variable, but its value at is the second joint moment of two random variables”.

3.3.3 Basic properties of the autocorrelation function

For the real number WSS process, the following holds.

(a) is average power

(b) Even function: merely swaps the roles of the two time points, so

(c) Maximum at the origin: Applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to

Therefore, the “typical ” is depicted as having a maximum value at and decreasing as increases. It is an intuition that the correlation with itself is strongest, and memory fades as time moves further away.

3.4 Wide-Sense Stationarity (WSS)

NoteDefinition (WSS)

A stochastic process is called WSST (WSST) if it satisfies the following two conditions.

  1. Average is constant:
  2. Autocorrelation depends only on time difference:

While SSS requires time-shift invariance of the joint distribution of all orders, WSS requires invariance of only the first and second moments. For this reason, WSS is also called second-order stationarity. To illustrate Condition 2: The PDFs themselves at times and may differ, but if the two points are shifted by the same amount , the correlation must be the same if the interval between the two points is the same.

TipQ. Why does hold in WSS?

This equation is not a theorem to be proven, but the definition of WSS itself (condition 2). It means “a process satisfying this property is called WSS.”

Question Answer
Does it automatically hold in a general stochastic process? No. In general, is a true 2-variable function
Does it hold within WSS? Yes. That is condition 2 of the WSS definition
Why is it valid to introduce such a condition? Since this condition is automatically derived when assuming SSS (as in the previous section), it is an independent assumption that extracts only the part actually necessary for PSD calculation from the conclusions of SSS and elevates it to an independent assumption.

Therefore, the moment of changing to in the subsequent Wiener–Khinchin derivation is not the moment of writing an identity, but the moment of introducing the decisive assumption that “this process is assumed to be WSS.”

3.4.1 The relationship between SSS and WSS

  • SSS ⇒ WSS: As shown above, the mean constant in and in Z depend only on . However, since itself is defined only if the second moment is finite, the condition is applied.
  • WSS ⇏ SSS: WSS imposes no constraints on joint distributions of degree 3 or higher. Counterexample (Discrete Time): If are independent of each other, and is if it is even and if it is odd, then the mean is always and the variance is always and , so it is WSS. However, since the marginal distribution itself changes with time, it is not SSS.
  • Exception: In Gaussian processes, WSS ⇔ SSS — Proven in the Gaussian process section.

In practice, WSS is often assumed even if it is not strictly SSS. For example, although radio channels are strictly time-varying, models that approximate WSS over short intervals (such as the WSSUS channel model) are used as a standard.

3.5 Covariance function and variance

The covariance function of the WSS process with mean is

It is . If expanded

That is, and have only a difference of a constant due to the mean, and they are identical when the mean is 0. is the non-centered second moment, and is the centered second moment.

Variance is the 0-lag value of the covariance function.

That is, the variance is the “squared mean of the degree to which deviates from the mean,” and is merely the value of the covariance function.

3.6 Examples satisfying SSS

Example 1: Stochastic Constant Process

This is a process that takes the same random variable as its value at all time points. For any , ,

Since , the joint distribution is trivially invariant. This is the simplest SSS example that holds regardless of the distribution of . The PSD for this process is calculated from.

Example 2: WSS Gaussian Process — Since the joint distribution of a Gaussian process is determined solely by the mean and covariance, if the mean and covariance are invariant to time shift (WSS), the entire joint distribution is invariant (SSS). This is proven in the Gaussian Process section. Gaussian white noise and exponentially correlated processes assumed to be Gaussian belong to this category.

NoteWhy Learn Normality
  1. Conceptual Reference Point: SSS provides a definition of “complete normality” and clarifies how much weaker the assumption of WSS used in practice is compared to it.
  2. Prerequisite for PSD Definition: PSD is defined as the Fourier transform of , and this definition holds if is a function of (at least WSS).
  3. Common Premise of Subsequent Theories: Subsequent models, such as the sampling theorem of band-limited processes and the stationary Poisson process ( constant), are also simplified based on the stationarity assumption.

4 Power Spectral Density

4.1 PSD of deterministic signals

The PSD of the deterministic signal is defined as the time average.

  • If spans an infinite amount of time, the total energy becomes infinite, so the Fourier transform can diverge.
  • So, we obtain the spectrum of the signal cut into the finite interval , and
  • After dividing (energy spectrum) by the observation interval length to convert it into power per unit time,
  • Send to to obtain the average power spectrum for the entire time.
TipQ. Is a period? Can’t the integration range be ? Why is the denominator ?

is not a period. This definition makes no assumption whatsoever about periodic signals; rather, it is intended to handle non-periodic signals and stochastic processes. is the half-window length of the observation interval, and the total length of the observation interval is . does not mean “the period goes infinitely,” but rather “the observation time is extended until it eventually reaches the average over the entire time axis”. (This confusion arises because the notation and appearance are similar to used for one period in Fourier series.)

The key principle is that the denominator equals the length of the integration interval. Only then will the result be an exact “per unit of time” amount.

Observation interval Interval length Normalization

Even if we set it as , it is a completely equivalent definition as long as normalization is maintained, and for the limit (for a normal signal), the starting point of the interval does not affect the result. Choosing an interval symmetric to the origin is for convenience of derivation. If we use the symmetric window , the integration region after the variable transformation below becomes a neat rhombus symmetric to the origin.

4.2 PSD of a stochastic process: Defined as expected value

The situation is different for the stochastic process .

  • The waveform varies depending on the sampling function, and what we know is not the waveform but only the distribution. The sample observed today is a different curve from the sample observed tomorrow.
  • Therefore, there is no single Fourier transform that represents the entire stochastic process. Although it is possible to calculate for a single sample function, its value is a random variable that differs for each sample.

Therefore, PSD is defined by calculating the finite interval spectrum and taking the ensemble mean (expected value). It averages the results so that each sampling function contributes by its own probability.

The result is the Wiener–Khinchin theorem.

In other words, the PSD of a stochastic process is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation function. This is derived step-by-step below.

4.3 Derivation of the Wiener–Khinchin theorem

4.3.1 Step 1: Set up a finite window

Observe a time-limited version to avoid convergence issues.

A finite amount of time is defined as follows.

4.3.2 Step 2: Expansion — Appearance of Complex Conjugates

The square of the absolute value of a complex number is the product of that number and its complex conjugate.

The first argument is the definition of , and the integration variable is written as . The second argument (conjugate) is written as another integration variable . Since is a real number, taking the conjugate only changes the sign of the exponent.

NoteReason for separating integration variables into and

The two factors must each have independent integration variables so that they can be combined into a double integral in the next step, where the product of two time points appears and connects to the autocorrelation . If only is used without a conjugate factor, the equality does not hold. The conjugate factor is the second integral.

4.3.3 Step 3: Convert the product of two integrals into a double integral

TipQ. Is there a guarantee that the product of the individual integrals is equal to the product followed by the integral?

It always holds true. It is an identity derived solely from the linearity of integration, not an approximation.

The key point is that after integration, and are not functions of , but constants (with respect to the given ).

(i) Since is a constant independent of , it can be substituted into the integral of .

(ii) is rewritten in its definition.

(iii) From the perspective of the inner integral, is a constant, so it is placed inside.

This result is strictly an iterated integral. Equating this to a double integral over a square region, and the justification for subsequent operations such as changing the order of integration or including in the integral, is guaranteed by the Fubini–Tonelli theorem.

If the integration interval is finite and the signal is bounded, this absolute convergence condition is automatically satisfied.

4.3.4 Step 4: Take the expected value and introduce the WSS assumption

Since both expectation and integral are linear operations (by Fubini), they can be interchanged.

Here we introduce a deterministic assumption: the process is WSS. Then is the autocorrelation function, and it depends only on the difference , not on the absolute time.

Now that the entire integrand has become a single function , it is natural to treat this difference as a new variable.

4.3.5 Step 5: Variable Transformation and Jacobian

The Jacobian determinant is

and the area element is

TipQ. It should be , so why is it ? Isn’t the symbol missing?

It is not an omission, but because the original absolute value is entered into the multivariable substitution integral formula.

  • and are area elements, and the area is always greater than or equal to 0 regardless of the coordinate system.
  • The sign of the determinant indicates whether the transformation preserves () or flips () the orientation, and the size indicates the scaling ratio of the area.
  • Since the area ratio is needed for integration, only is used.

Here, is obtained because the winding direction of the axis is reversed, as decreases as increases. If defined as , is obtained. In either case, since it is , this transformation preserves the area, and can be used as is.

4.3.6 Step 6: Integration Region — The square becomes a rhombus

The original integration region is a square . We move this to .

① Condition

② Condition

③ Intersection of two conditions: Take the larger of the lower bounds and the smaller of the upper bounds.

④ Range of : For the interval not to be empty, lower bound ≤ upper bound must be true.

Therefore

is a diamond in the plane. The transformation is equivalent to rotating a square to make the diagonal the new axis, so the original square appears as a rhombus in the new coordinates. As goes from to , the allowable width decreases linearly to become a vertex.

4.3.7 Step 7: Integrate for — Introduction of trigonometric weights

Since the integrand does not depend on , the integration is merely to find the “height (width)” of the rhombus.

If you divide by

NoteMeaning of triangular weights

Within an observation interval of length , the number of pairs of points with a time difference Z is highest at , and decreases linearly as increases (width of the rhombus). That is, in finite observations, correlation of large lags is less reflected, and this effect is represented by triangular (Bartlett) weights.

4.3.8 8th step: extreme

If , then at each it becomes and the integration interval expands to .

(The exchange between limits and integrals is justified by the Governing Convergence Theorem if . When includes a delta function, as in white noise, it is understood in the sense of a generalized function.)

4.4 Wiener–Khinchin pairs and properties

Time delay structure ⇔ frequency component are a Fourier pair with each other. From this, several properties emerge immediately.

  • Total Power: Substituting into the inverse transform yields . Integrating the PSD over the entire frequency range gives the average power.
  • Real-Even Function: Since is a real-even function, is a real-even function and is an even function for .
  • Non-negative: is the limit of , so it is .

5 Example: Correlation Structure and Spectrum Duality

5.1 Extreme 1 — White Noise:

In communication, is usually used instead of : , (both PSD).

Statistical Significance: From different perspectives

In other words, if the two points in time differ even slightly, the correlation is 0. It is a no memory process, so even if you know the exact value at any given moment, you cannot predict the value a very short time later.

NotePhysical example: thermal noise

If you measure the voltage across a resistor with no power connected, it appears as zero on a large scale, but if you zoom in with an oscilloscope to the level, it is not exactly zero. This is because the numerous electrons inside the conductor move randomly due to thermal energy, shifting to one side at one moment and to the opposite side the next. The average is zero, but the instantaneous value fluctuates between positive and negative.

  • Why White: Even if we know the noise at a single moment, we cannot predict the noise seconds later. Since it does not matter, it is , and the PSD is the same whether it is 100 MHz or several GHz. This is the reason why we cannot control or predict this noise.
  • Why Gaussian: Since the noise voltage is the sum of a very large number of electron motions, by the central limit theorem, the overall behavior appears as a Gaussian random variable with a mean of 0.
  • Origin of the Name: It is called “white” by likening it to light that appears white when all visible frequency components are evenly mixed. However, this is merely a metaphor for the name; the actual solar spectrum is in the form of blackbody radiation and is not strictly flat.
WarningThe point of idealization

Perfect white noise is , meaning average power is infinite, so it is a mathematical idealization that cannot physically exist. Since actual thermal noise is flat at room temperature up to approximately , the white model is used to mean that it is flat over a much wider range than the band of interest (radio communication band). After passing through the receiver filter, the power becomes finite (see LTI section below).

5.2 Extreme 2 — Stochastic Constant Process:

5.2.1 Autocorrelation

Since the same random variable is at all times, no matter what the time is or what is

TipQ. Why ?

Definition of variance (where ) expands

Therefore . That is, it is the identity second moment = variance + square of the mean. has been rewritten using two more familiar statistics (mean, variance).

Perfect correlation across all lags — This process has full memory. If you know the value at one moment, you know the values at all times.

5.2.2 PSD: The Fourier transform of a constant is a delta function

If you say

(Generally, if it is , it is .)

TipQ. Why does this integral become ?

Since the integrand oscillates with a magnitude of 1 at , this integral does not exist as an ordinary (absolutely convergent) integral. It must be understood in the sense of a limit (distribution).

Calculate first in a finite interval

If we view this function as a function of , it has the following properties in .

  1. Area is always 1: (Independent of , Dirichlet integral )
  2. Origin height diverges: Value at
  3. Cancels in : oscillates increasingly faster, so averaging over small intervals results in 0, which vanishes.

The width is fixed at 1, the depth goes to 0, and the height goes to infinity — this is exactly the defining property of Dirac delta.

Verification via inverse transformation: , which matches the original .

This result is consistent with the physical intuition that an unchanging signal has all its power in direct current (DC, ).

NoteNote: Normal but not ergodic

The process is SSS, but the time mean of a single sample function is , which is a random variable and is generally different from the ensemble mean . In other words, it is a prime example where it is impossible to determine ensemble statistics (ergodicity) by observing a single sample for a long time. Stationarity and ergodicity are distinct properties.

5.3 Compromise — Exponential Correlation and Lorentzian PSD

Consider exponential autocorrelation with mean 0 and correlation time .

5.3.1 Step 1: Divide the interval due to absolute value and combine with cosine

If we substitute into the first integral, the interval changes to and

Therefore, by Euler’s formula

This is an example of the general property that “The Fourier transform of an even function can be computed using the cosine transform”.

5.3.2 Step 2: Standard Integral

Proof: Since

(Since , damping occurs at ). If you take the real part

5.3.3 Step 3: Substitution and Organization

If you substitute , and multiply the numerator and denominator by

Verification: Total power ✓. Half power (−3 dB) frequency is .

5.4 Duality Theorem

The three examples lie on the spectrum of time–frequency duality.

Process (Time Domain) (Frequency Domain) Memory
White Noise — Infinitely narrow — Infinitely wide (flat) None
Exponential Correlation — Width Lorentzian — Width Finite
Probability constant — Infinitely wide (constant) — Infinitely narrow Perfect

As it spreads widely in the region, it narrows in the region. Exponential correlation is an intermediate step that approaches white noise at and a stochastic constant at .

6 Stochastic process passing through the LTI system

6.1 LTI System Review

In a system with an impulse response of

  • Linear: The Principle of Superposition —
  • Time-invariant: The same input yields the same output (shifted by time) whether input is given today or tomorrow — the system’s impulse response does not change over time.

If , the output is the convolution of the input and the impulse response.

6.2 Problem Settings

Now, instead of the deterministic signal, we put the WSS stochastic process into a stable LTI filter.

While is a deterministic function, is a stochastic process where only the distribution is known at each time step; therefore, the waveform of itself cannot be obtained. Instead, we calculate the output statistics (mean, autocorrelation, PSD). The goal is…

and this shows that the output is also WSS.

NoteIntuitive Approach

Looking at according to the definition of PSD, since convolution is a product in the frequency domain, it is , and is deterministic and comes out of the expectation value. Then it becomes , and we immediately obtain . Due to the boundary effects of the finite window, this is not a rigorous derivation (the boundary effects disappear in ), and below, we follow a rigorous path through autocorrelation. The key point is that it is the same calculation as for the deterministic signal, but with only the expectation value applied.

6.3 Output Average

By exchanging expectation and integral

is a time-independent constant. (If the input mean is 0, the output mean is also 0.)

6.4 Derivation of output autocorrelation

Starting from the definition, apply the convolution form to and .

Using the linearity of expectation (Tonelli/Fubini), is placed into the integral, and since the input is WSS, :

Separating lag by variable conversion: Set to

Each argument is

, and since the absolute value of the Jacobian of is 1,

Since no remains on the right side, the output autocorrelation depends only on . Since the mean was also a constant, the output is WSS.

Grouping by : If we first perform the integration of for a fixed

If you just change the variable name and use it from the origin

, that is, is the convolution of and the time-inverted . Using this, the output autocorrelation is the convolution over the lag .

6.5 Frequency range:

We apply the convolution theorem (time convolution ⇔ frequency product) to Wiener–Khinchin(). Since for the real ,

The LTI filter shapes the input PSD into the argument . It is also worth noting that the phase information has no effect on the PSD at all.

6.6 White noise input

If the input is ,

TipQ. Why did the convolution symbol in the middle, , disappear?

It has not disappeared; rather, since the convolution with the delta function is the identity operation, it was calculated immediately without integration. Let

If we apply the sifting property of the delta function to

Just as multiplying by 1 in multiplication does not change anything, in convolution, is the identity element (). within the remaining remains as it is because it is a distinct convolution contained in the definition of itself.

In other words, when flat white noise passes through a filter, the shape of the output PSD becomes exactly the shape of the filter . The previously mentioned problem of the white noise having infinite power is resolved as passes through an integrable (band-limited) filter, resulting in .

7 Wiener Process

7.1 Definition

The process of integrating the white noise ZZZPH0002092ZZZ (, , ) is called the Wiener process.

Intuition: Continuous-time random walk. The value at time is the cumulative sum of infinitesimal random kicks received from white noise from the start to that time. Since the waveform of white noise can be infinitely numerous, taking one shape with some probability and that shape with others, is also a stochastic process.

7.2 Average

Since both integrals and expectations are linear operators, they are interchangeable.

Since it is an accumulation of inputs with an average of 0, it is a centered process that does not drift to one side.

7.3 Derivation of Autocorrelation

About

(For convenience, the order of integration is written as and .) If we substitute

TipQ. Why does the integration range change from to ?

Calculate the inner integral first. The field property is originally , but here the integration interval is restricted to . If the delta “peak” is inside the interval, it is 1, and if it is outside, it is 0.

The outer integral counts the length of the part inside at the same time while scans .

Since both intervals start at 0, the intersection is always to the shorter endpoint.

  • :
  • :
  • In any case , length

Geometric Figure: In the plane, the region of integration is a rectangle , and has a value only on the diagonal . Therefore, the double integral is the length of the part of the rectangle where the diagonal is contained (on an appropriate scale), and since the diagonal starting from the origin ends at the shorter side of the rectangle first, its length is . In this way, thanks to the field property, the double integral collapses into a much simpler single integral.

7.4 The Winner process is not a normal process

depends on the absolute time and cannot be expressed solely by the difference . For example, if , it becomes , and if , it becomes ; thus, the values are different even though is the same. Therefore, the WSS condition is violated, and the Wiener process is non-stationary.

Especially if set to , the variance is

increases linearly in proportion to time. Since random shocks continue to accumulate, the spread becomes increasingly larger. The normalized correlation coefficient is

depends on the ratio of the two times.

WarningWhy is the previous “WSS input → LTI → WSS output” result not applied?

The reason the output is not WSS when inputting white noise of WSS into a linear operation called “integration” is that this operation does not satisfy the assumption in the previous section.

  1. Not time-invariant: has an integral starting point that is a fixed origin 0. Since the integral starting point does not move even when the input is shifted in time, it is not a time-invariant system. The fact that it “started at time 0” itself creates absolute time information.
  2. Not stable: The ideal integrator is not BIBO stable with , and formally is not integrable near . Integrating results in infinite power, which corresponds to the phenomenon where the variance increases infinitely with .

7.5 Independent Incremental and Gaussian Marginal Distribution

Independent increments: The increments in non-overlapping intervals are unrelated. For

Intuitively, and use only the non-overlapping intervals of white noise, because white noise is uncorrelated at different times. If is Gaussian, then non-correlation is independence, so the increments are independent.

Gaussian Marginal Distribution: If is Gaussian white noise, then it is . This is directly connected to the Gaussian process in the next section.

8 Gaussian Process

8.1 Definition

NoteDefinition

The stochastic process is Gaussian for a random finite set of times of which a probability vector

This means that follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution.

You must pay attention to the weight of the condition “arbitrary”.

  • : No matter which time is selected, is (univariate) Gaussian
  • : If two times are selected, is a 2D Gaussian
  • Any , no matter which perspective is chosen, it is always a multivariate Gaussian
NoteSimilar in format to SSS but different conditions

The definitions of SSS and Gaussian processes are similar in form in that they are joint distribution conditions for “arbitrary , arbitrary time”. However

  • SSS: Is the joint distribution invariant to time shifts?
  • Gaussian: Does the joint distribution belong to the Gaussian distribution family?

By asking for , the two conditions are independent of each other. Being Gaussian does not mean it is normal, nor does being normal mean it is Gaussian.

8.2 Completely determined by mean and covariance alone

The multivariate Gaussian distribution is a special family of distributions that is completely determined by only the mean vector and the covariance matrix.

Therefore, all statistical information of the Gaussian process is summarized by only two functions.

With just these two functions, you can calculate joint distributions of any order, from 3rd to 4th, … and so on. This is why the Gaussian process is “very important and widely used.”

8.3 WSS Gaussian process is SSS

Let the Gaussian process be WSS, i.e., and . If we shift all time points by ,

  • Mean vector: — Invariant
  • Covariance matrix: — Invariant

Since both factors determining the joint distribution are invariant, the entire joint distribution is invariant, i.e., it is SSS.

In general processes, WSS cannot constrain distributions of order 3 or higher, but since the entire distribution of a Gaussian is determined by only the first and second moments from the outset, second-order stationarity is lifted up to total stationarity. Due to this property, Gaussian white noise is SSS.

8.4 Closed for linear operations

The Gaussian process remains Gaussian even after undergoing the following linear operation.

  • Differentiation and Integration (where defined)
  • LTI Filtering
  • Sampling in discrete time
  • Sum with other (combined) Gaussian processes

The basis is the fact that “a linear combination of Gaussian random variables is Gaussian,” and integration and filtering are linear combinations in the sense of limits. Therefore

The output of a linear system driven by a Gaussian process is Gaussian.

Combined with the result from the previous section: When a WSS Gaussian input passes through a stable LTI filter, the output is WSS Gaussian = SSS, and its distribution is completely determined by and . This is why the noise in the receiver filter output can be treated as Gaussian.

8.5 Relationship with the Winner Process

The Wiener process is a representative example of a Gaussian process (Brownian motion). The reason is as follows:

  1. In , integration is a linear operation.
  2. If input is Gaussian white noise, then at a finite number of times is a (limited) linear combination of Gaussian random variables.
  3. Therefore, satisfies the definition of a multivariate Gaussian-Gaussian process.

Practical Advantage: Since the Wiener process is Gaussian, all finite-dimensional joint distributions can be determined using only the two previously calculated means and . For example, the distribution of is

is immediately determined as a bivariate Gaussian.

ImportantStationarity and Gaussianity are independent properties
Properties Wiener Process Basis
Stationarity (WSS/SSS) ✗ Does not hold depends on absolute time
Gaussian process ✓ Holds (when the input is Gaussian) The linear operation called integration preserves Gaussianity

The Wiener process is a representative example of a “Gaussian but not stationary” process, and the stochastic constant process (where is non-Gaussian) is an example of a “stationary but not Gaussian” process. The theorem that the WSS and SSS coincide in a Gaussian process applies only when it is Gaussian and simultaneously WSS, and since the Wiener process does not have a WSS, this does not apply.

9 Key Summary

Concept Key Formula One-line Summary
Stochastic process Fixed → Sample function, Fixed → Random variable
SSS Joint distribution of all orders is invariant to time shifts
WSS Only the 1st and 2nd moments are invariant (definition and assumption)
Autocorrelation Even function,
Covariance Second moment minus the mean
PSD Ensemble average of finite interval spectra
Wiener–Khinchin Conjugate expansion → Double integral → WSS → Rhombus → Trigonometric weighting → Limit
White Noise No Memory, Flat Spectrum
Probability constant Perfect memory, power concentrated in DC
Exponential Correlation Time Width ↔︎ Frequency Width
LTI Output Filter shapes PSD into , output is also WSS
Wiener process Abnormal, Variance , Independent Incremental
Gaussian process Any is completely determined by a multivariate Gaussian , closed to linear operations, WSS⇔SSS

item.title: Stochastic Processes - II
item.description:
1 Overall flow

This document is composed of two branches.

  1. Sampling: Multiplying a continuous-time signal by an impulse train replicates the spectrum in the frequency domain at intervals of . When applied to a random process, a band-limited steady-state process is represented as a discrete-time random sequence without loss.
  2. Poisson Process: A point process that models “events whose timing is unknown.” From the small- law, it is derived that the number of events within an interval follows a Poisson distribution.

Both topics have in common that they deal with points on the time axis. In sampling, points are placed on a deterministic lattice , while in the Poisson process, the positions of the points themselves are random.

2 Impulse Column Sampling

2.1 Definition

impulse train with period

If defined as , sampling is the product of the signal and the impulse train.

The second equality comes from . The sample value is stored as the area of each impulse.

2.2 Fourier Series Review

To obtain the Fourier transform of an impulse train, a Fourier series is required.

Orthogonality. When the periods are and , the complex exponent is orthogonal over one period.

If , the integral is 0 because it rotates an integer number of times during one period, and if , the integrand is 1.

When both sides of Coefficient. are multiplied by and integrated over one period, only the term remains.

NoteSource of

is the basis norm squared . It has the same structure as the expanded coefficient of an orthogonal basis in finite dimensions, . is the one-period average (DC component).

2.3 Fourier transform of complex exponential:

The transformation pair is set to the following convention.

For , the defining expression does not converge in the classical sense because the absolute value of the integrand is 1. Therefore, we consider a candidate and verify it using the inverse transform. Let .

Interpretation. The spectrum of a signal rotating forever at a single frequency exists only at that single point of frequency. The coefficient is a value that compensates for the convention of the inverse transform. In particular, if , then .

Meaning as a distribution. If the integral is cut at

This function tapers at with height and width , and the area is fixed at . Therefore, the limit when integrating over the test function is , and the equation should be understood in this sense.

2.4 Fourier transform of an impulse train

① Fourier Series. has a period , and within one period , there is only one impulse . Due to the sifting property

All harmonic components have the same magnitude and phase, so they simultaneously undergo constructive interference only at to create an impulse.

② Term-wise transformation. If you use linearity and the above result

In general, if the series coefficient of a periodic signal is , then it is . That is, the position of the impulse is , and the area is .

2.4.1 Coefficient Dissection

Since is already in the formula, the preceding coefficient may appear redundant, but the two have different roles.

Element Role Source
of Position of impulse Period → Fundamental frequency
Part of the preceding impulse area Fourier series coefficients
Part of the preceding impulse area area transformation convention ()

Since the area is numerically equal to , writing is equivalent. In this case, the preceding represents the area, not the location.

Assuming there are no coefficients leads to a contradiction. Letting and performing the inverse transform, by the Poisson sum formula

2.4.2 Verification

  • Dimension: The unit of is , and passing through , the transformation is dimensionless. The right-hand side is also dimensionless.
  • Notation: . In the convention, it is , so . If changed to , it matches the result of the range. That is, is a product of the notation convention, and is the intrinsic scale.

2.5 Spectrum of the sampled signal

The product in the time domain is the convolution in the frequency domain ( is attached in the convention ).

of is canceled out by the of the convolution, and the remaining becomes the gain of each replica. The original spectrum is replicated at intervals.

2.6 Aliasing and Full Restoration

Let’s call it for .

  • : The duplicates do not overlap. If only the baseband duplicates are selected using an ideal low-pass filter (LPF), is restored.
  • : Adjacent copies overlap (aliasing). Since the original component and the duplicate component are added together at the overlapping part, they cannot be separated by any filter.
TipDetailed conditions of the restoration filter

Since the gain of the replica is , the passband gain of the LPF must be to accurately recover the original signal.

The cutoff frequency can be placed anywhere in the empty band between the two copies, not just . If set to , it becomes (normalized sinc) and yields the interpolation formula .

3 Sampling of Random Processes and Random Sequences

3.1 Random Sequence

A random sequence is a random process with integer time indices, that is, a discrete-time random process.

Sampling the continuous-time process at intervals results in a random sequence.

3.2 Sampling Theorem for Random Processes

For deterministic signals, we examined whether the Fourier transform is band-limited. Since the sample path of a random process usually has infinite energy and therefore no Fourier transform exists, we use the Power Spectral Density (PSD) as the reference.

ImportantCleanup

WSS If the process satisfies for and the sample interval is , then the discrete-time sequence represents the original process.

Here, “expresses” does not mean point-by-point convergence of individual sample paths, but mean-square in the sense of

This means that holds. The difference from the deterministic sampling theorem is that the concept of stochastic convergence is required in random processes.

3.3 Correlation function of a sampled sequence

For the WSS process , depends only on the lag . The correlation function of the sampled sequence is

In the final equality, the WSS property (depending only on the lag , independent of ) was applied. Therefore, is also a WSS sequence, and its correlation function is the continuous correlation function sampled at intervals of .

3.4 PSD of sampled sequence: Probabilistic version of spectral replication

The PSD of a sequence at normalized frequency (cycles/sample) is defined as the discrete-time Fourier transform.

If you substitute and use the Poisson sum formula

is exactly the same structure as the deterministic signal . is limited to , and if it is , the copies do not overlap, so can be read back from . This is the frequency domain meaning of the PSD reference sampling theorem.

4 Poisson Process: Definition and Basic Properties

4.1 Point process and counting process

A point process is a mathematical model of a random event occurring at a specific point in time (or space). Examples: the arrival time of a packet in a network, the position of a star on the celestial sphere.

Taking packet arrival as an example, the arrival time is random because it is impossible to know exactly when the user will send the next request. This is described in terms of two quantities.

  • Counting Process : Start of observation. Number of events that occurred from to . .
  • Event Time : The time when the -th event occurred. The vector containing event times up to is written as (the dimension itself is random).

The interval coefficient is obtained from the difference of the cumulative coefficients.

4.1.1 interval endpoint convention

Depending on how is defined, whether the endpoint of the interval counted by is included depends on the definition.

Definition Continuity of the sample path Interval counted by
(“”, standard) accidental genus (càdlàg)
Left Continuous

“number of events occurring up to ” is consistent with the properties of the coincidence, and is the one that matches. Although some formulas in this document are written as by convention, since event times in a Poisson process follow a continuous distribution (), the distributions of the two conventions are identical. The difference becomes an actual issue in general point processes or discrete-time models where events can be clustered at deterministic times (e.g., slot boundaries). Regardless of the convention, the interval must be standardized to a semi-open interval so that adjacent intervals are partitioned without overlap or omission, as in .

4.2 Properties of the sample path

The sample path of (=) is a step function and has the following properties.

  • Non-decrease: The number of events only increases or remains the same and does not decrease.
  • Integer value: Since it counts events
  • Casual: The count is updated to a new value the very moment the event occurs. .
  • Unit Jump: at each jump time.
  • Between events, is constant.

4.2.1 Why Unit Jumps: Orderliness

“One event increments the count by exactly 1” is merely the definition of the counting process (weight of 1 for each event). The jump size is

Since , if two events overlap at the same time, the jump becomes 2. In fact, there exist non-simple point processes that allow batch arrival. Therefore, for a “unit jump” to hold, the property that at most one event at a time is additionally required, and the Poisson process guarantees this under the following condition.

Proof (Probability of simultaneous events = 0). Divide into Z subintervals of length . By the union bound

Since two events at the same time fall into the same subinterval in any partition, the probability of this happening is less than this upper bound and is 0. In other words, almost certainly (as) all event times are different.

Another perspective. As shown later, the arrival interval follows an exponential distribution (continuous distribution), so it is .

In models where co-arrival is actually important, the compound Poisson process is used. The arrival times are Poisson, and the jump size of each arrival follows a random distribution.

4.3 Intensity and Infinitesimal Interval Law

The probability law of a point process is defined by strength . For a sufficiently small

Symbol Meaning
Number of events in the infinitesimal interval

Instantaneous occurrence rate, unit is events/s
In Hang

Intuition: Speed × Time. Just as traveling at a speed of for a time of results in a distance of , if the occurrence rate is for a time of , the probability of an event is approximately (dimensionless). For example, if /s, ms, the probability is approximately .

does not determine the number of events. /s does not mean that exactly 10 events occur in 2 seconds. is a quantity that determines the probability in an infinitesimal interval, and the actual number is random (we will show later that the average is ).

Read as definition of intensity.

The idea is similar to giving the probability of a small interval , but since is not a density but a rate, it can be greater than 1. must be sufficiently small so that it becomes .

Why is it and not an equal sign? In the Poisson process of constant intensity , exactly

. is a first-order approximation, and the rest are of a higher order than and are ignored compared to .

4.3.1 Notation: ; and ,

In , , ; and , have mathematically the same role (all arguments/conditions), and the only difference is the notational grouping.

  • , : List of factors at the same level
  • ; : The first part is the current status , and the second part is the history , distinguishing the roles.

That is, and . For reference, since , is information determined from .

; conventions in other fields meaning

, Distinguishing two variables in mutual information; \mid is the condition

Here, is not a fixed parameter but a random history, so it differs from the convention. In point process literature, the same object is often written as the conditional strength for the history .

4.3.2 Classification of point processes according to intensity function

Strength Process Example
Normal (Uniform) Poisson Packet arrival with constant average traffic
Abnormal (Non-vehicle) Poisson Traffic change by time of day (Day ↑, Night ↓)
depends on self-excitation process (Hawkes et al.) earthquake aftershock, burst traffic

The infinitesimal interval law is a framework that defines the intensity of not only Poisson processes but the entire point process, and a Poisson process is a case where the intensity does not depend on hysteresis.

4.4 Normal Poisson Process and Abnormal Poisson Process

The Poisson process is memoryless: its strength does not depend on the process history .

  • Stationary: (Constant). Independent of time and history.
  • nonstationary: . It changes over time but is still unrelated to history.

Interpretation of Coin Toss. Divide the time axis into squares, and for each square, toss a coin that produces an “event” with probability . Each toss is independent of past (and future) results. In the case of anomalies, only the probability changes to in the square at time , while the independence remains the same.

WarningDistinguish between “normal” and “independent”

The source of independence between intervals is memorylessness (hysteresis-independence), not stationarity (constant strength). Even in an anomalous Poisson process, the number of events in non-overlapping intervals is independent of each other. This is the reason why the derivation of the count statistics that follows holds true in the general form .

4.5 Two Laws of Probability

  1. count statistics: The probability that there are events in the interval .
  2. Time of occurrence: Joint distribution of the times of the first events within the observation interval .

4.5.1 Why the time of occurrence is important

Information inclusion relationship. The count is a function of time.

If the joint distribution of event times is known, the count distribution of any interval is determined, but the count distribution alone cannot tell where the events are clustered within the interval. For example, the information that there are “2” in cannot distinguish between (burst) and (variance). The time distribution is a complete description of the process, and the count is a summary of it.

Meaning in communication systems.

  • Queueing Delay: Even if the average arrival rate is the same, a queue builds up if arrival times are concentrated.
  • Collision Probability (ALOHA type): Whether two transmissions overlap depends not on the number of times but on the time difference .
  • Estimation/Testing: The likelihood used to estimate the maximum likelihood of with the observed event times or to test the Poisson assumption is the joint density of the times.

The reason count statistics are derived first is that they are simpler summaries, not because the time of occurrence is less important. The rule of the time of occurrence is derived from the count results in the distribution of arrival times .

Objective: In a Poisson process (including abnormal) with intensity

Note notation arithmetic

5.7 Result Verification

Normalization. . ✓

Mean and Variance (Derivative of the Generating Function).

Mean = Variance = . Since the mean in the normal case is , the interpretation that “ = average number of events per unit time” is justified here. As the standard deviation decreases to relative to the mean , the number is relatively concentrated around the mean over long intervals.

5.8 Extreme behavior: When the interval and grow together

What happens to the individual probability mass when (the interval is very long or the intensity is high)?

6 Distribution of arrival times

The fact that the first event occurs after is the same as saying that there is no event in .

9 Commonly confused points

  1. Are and duplicates? No. The numerical values are the same, but one is the impulse area and the other is the position. If you subtract the area, the inverse transformation becomes times.
  2. vs ? The one that fits is . There is no difference in distribution during the Poisson process.

item.title: Stochastic Processes - III
item.description:
1 Introduction

1.1 Two questions addressed by stochastic signal theory

When dealing only with deterministic signals , , it was sufficient to analyze the signal itself. However, actual observations are usually

It is in the form , and here two questions arise.

  1. Noise is a stochastic process. What is a stochastic process, what characteristics (mean, autocorrelation, distribution) describe it, and what tools are used to analyze it?
  2. The signal itself can be probabilistic. For example, , whose phase follows a uniform distribution, is not a deterministic function but a stochastic process. To estimate parameters based solely on observations , or to detect whether came from the hypothesis or , the basis of stochastic processes is required.

This document covers the Poisson process among its foundations.

1.2 Sampling Theorem Review (Brief)

When a baseband spectrum with a bandwidth of is sampled at a sampling frequency , if , the duplicated spectra do not overlap, so the original baseband spectrum can be restored using a low-pass filter. Otherwise, aliasing occurs where the duplicated spectra overlap.

The reason is that sampling is a multiplication with an impulse train in the time domain, and since the Fourier transform of an impulse train is an impulse train again, in the frequency domain it becomes a convolution between the original spectrum and the impulse train, i.e., a spectral replication at the interval.

1.3 Two Perspectives on the Poisson Process

Perspective Question Random Variable Range of Values Description of Distribution
Count statistics How many events occurred in the interval ? PMF (Probability Mass Function)
Time of occurrence When did the event happen? Ordered real numbers PDF (Probability density function)

If the counting process is plotted over time, it becomes a staircase that starts at 0 and rises one step at a time for each event. The arrival time is the point at which each step rises. The only difference is whether the same realization is read as “height” or “corner position,” but the two perspectives describe the same object.

ImportantDo not mix PMF and PDF

Since is an integer value, is the probability itself. On the other hand, since is a continuous real value, it is , and the meaningful quantity is the density . Probability is obtained by multiplying the density by the infinitesimal volume: . The sample function density , which will appear later, is a mixed form that is the PMF for and the PDF for .

The first part (Chapters 2–5) deals with count statistics, and the second part (Chapters 6–9) deals with time of occurrence.

2 Definition of Poisson Process and Count Distribution

2.1 Infinitesimal interval axiom

The Poisson coefficient process with intensity (rate) is defined by the following three properties.

Axiom 1 (Independent Increments). Counts of non-overlapping intervals are independent of each other.

Axiom 2 (Strength). The probability that exactly 1 event occurs in an interval of length is

Axiom 3 (Scarcity, Orderliness). The probability of two or more occurrences in the same interval is

Here, represents the term satisfying , i.e., the remainder that approaches zero faster than . Automatically from Axioms 2 and 3.

Intuition. In very short periods, there is at most one event, and the probability is linearly proportional to the length of time.

2.2 Meaning of Homogeneous

Homogeneous means that the intensity is homogeneous with respect to time, that is, , meaning that all points on the time axis are equal.

  • HPP (Homogeneous Poisson Process): (constant)
  • NHPP (Non-Homogeneous Poisson Process): is a function of time

“Homogeneity” means that statistical properties do not change even when the time axis is shifted, which corresponds to the stationary increments property that will be discussed later. This is in the same context as a homogeneous Markov chain, which refers to a chain where “transition probabilities do not depend on time.”

2.3 Derivation of PMF: Limit of Binomial Distribution

Let’s divide into Z pieces of length . By the axioms, the count of each piece is (approximately) 0 or 1 and The pieces are independent of each other. Therefore, and

If you fix and send it to :

  • (i)·(ii)
    1. (Standard limit )

This is the law of rare events where “number of trials , probability of success , mean fixed”.

Reason why occurrences of 2 or more can be ignored. The sum of the probabilities of “2 or more in any piece” across the entire interval is Since , the approximation “each piece is 0 or 1” becomes accurate in the limit .

2.4 Section Count

HPP. Since it is due to normal increment, you just need to change to .

Consistency check. In , the two terms are independent, and by Poisson’s additivity, becomes exactly the same as .

Insert cumulative intensity in place of NHPP. .

Why integration? If the interval is divided into infinitesimal pieces , each piece is an independent Bernoulli , and the average of the sum is . If it is , it returns to , so HPP is a special case. Also, if we set it to , it becomes , which has the same structure as the increment of the count .

3 Mean, Variance, Generating Function

3.1 Average: Calculated directly as a series

  1. The term is 0 because of the preceding , so the sum starts from .
  2. Take out and move the exponent to .
  3. If you use the exponential series

Interpretation. Expected count = Intensity × Time. The larger is, and the longer the observation time, the more events are observed.

3.2 Probability Generating Function (PGF)

3.2.1 Definition and Three Properties

For a non-negative integer random variable is a power series with probability masses as coefficients and always converges at .

(3) The PGF of an independent sum is the product of PGFs. If

Method B: From the structure of the process. If is divided into pieces, it becomes , and by independent increments, are independent. 3.3 Variance

To PGF. Since , , and Since the exponential function maintains its form when differentiated, the factorial moment of degree is regardless of how many times it is differentiated.

Directly as a series. If split into Since the term is 0 in , the sum starts from , , and the term becomes in the same way,
